Consider the work of God: who can make straight what He has made crooked? - Ecclesiastes 7:13

Scripture is quoted from the Berean Standard Bible, kept closer to the author’s own Bible where his argument rests on its wording; capitals for God in quotations (He, His) follow the BSB. “You+” marks every plural “you” (the older “ye”); a plain “you” is singular or general.

To the Reader

A habitual unwillingness to be reconciled to the cross, and an obvious deficiency in many of the duties that belong to us as members of the body of Christ, greatly mar our Christian comfort, our edification, and our usefulness. Instead of adorning our holy profession of faith, they cast a dark shadow on it. As a remedy in both cases, the Lord in his kind providence is sending us fresh help in the two treatises that follow. Both subjects are set in a new and engaging light. It is right that the reader should know that the first of them, that of the crook in one’s lot, was among the last subjects the blessed author handled, and that revising it as far as he did (for he did not get through all his notes) was among his last works with the pen. We leave it to the reader’s attention to judge how far he revised it himself, and where we have only his notes as he preached them. The author often and earnestly sought God’s blessing on anything of his that was, or should be, brought out for the service of the church. May that same divine blessing go along with these treatises that follow.

Part I: The Crook in the Lot

Eccl 7:13.

Consider the work of God: who can make straight what He has made crooked?

A just view of afflicting events is altogether necessary for Christian conduct under them, and that view is to be had only by faith, not by sight. For it is the light of the word alone that represents them justly, revealing in them the work of God, and so purposes worthy of the divine perfections. When these are perceived by the eye of faith and duly considered, a man has a just view of afflicting events, one fitted to quell the turbulent movements of corrupt affections under dismal outward appearances.

It is with this view that Solomon, in the earlier part of this chapter, puts forward several paradoxes. They are surprising judgments in favor of certain things that look gloomy and hideous to sight, and are therefore generally thought grievous and shocking. He pronounces one’s day of death to be better than his day of birth: that is, the day of death of one who, having become the friend of God through faith, has led a life to the honor of God and the service of his generation, and so has gained for himself the good and fragrant name that is better than fine perfume (v. 1). In the same way he pronounces the house of mourning better than the house of feasting, sorrow better than laughter, and a wise man’s rebuke better than the song of fools. For though the latter are indeed more pleasant, the former are more profitable (vv. 2–6). He observes with concern how men are in danger not only from the world’s frowns and ill treatment, oppression turning a wise man into a fool, but also from its smiles and caresses, a gift corrupting the heart. So, since there is danger whichever way it goes, he pronounces the end of every worldly matter better than its beginning (vv. 7, 8). And from the whole he rightly concludes that it is better to be humble and patient than proud and impatient under afflicting dispensations. For in the first case a man wisely submits to what is really best; in the second he fights against it (v. 8). He warns us against being angry with our lot because of the adversity found in it (v. 9). He cautions against making odious comparisons between former and present times, which on that point hint at unjust aspersions on the providence of God (v. 10). And against that complaining and fretful disposition he first prescribes a general remedy, namely, holy wisdom, as what enables a man to make the best of everything, and even preserves life in killing circumstances (vv. 11, 12). Then he prescribes a particular remedy, which consists in a right application of that wisdom to taking a just view of the case: “Consider the work of God: who can make straight what He has made crooked?”

In these words are set out (1.) the remedy itself, and (2.) its suitableness. First, the remedy itself is a wise eyeing of the hand of God in all that we find bearing hard on us: “Consider the work” (or, “See the doing”) “of God,” that is, in the crooked, rough, and disagreeable parts of your lot, the crosses you find in it. You see the cross itself very well. Indeed, you turn it over and over in your mind and view it at leisure on all sides. You look as well to this or that second cause of it, and so you are in a foam and a fret. But if you want to be quieted and satisfied in the matter, lift up your eyes toward heaven and see the doing of God in it, the working of his hand. Look at that, and consider it well. Look to the first cause of the crook in your lot; see how it is the work of God, his doing. Secondly, as for the suitableness of this remedy, that view of the crook in our lot is very suitable to still unseemly risings of heart and to quiet us under it: “who can” (that is, no one can) “make straight what” God “has made crooked?” As for the crook in your lot, God has made it, and it must continue as long as he wills it so. If you should put out your utmost strength to even it, or make it straight, your attempt will be in vain. It will not change for all you can do; only he who made it can mend it, or make it straight. This consideration, this view of the matter, is a proper means at once to silence and to satisfy men, and so to bring them to a dutiful submission to their Maker and Governor under the crook in their lot.

Now we take up the purpose of the text in these three doctrines. I. Whatever crook there is in one’s lot, it is of God’s making. II. What God sees fit to mar in one’s lot, one will not be able to mend. III. Considering the crook in the lot as the work of God, or of his making, is a proper means to bring one to Christian conduct under it.

Doctrine I.

Whatever crook is in one’s lot, it is of God’s making.

Here two things are to be considered, namely, the crook itself, and God’s making it.

I. As to the crook itself, the crook in the lot, these few things are set down first, for a better understanding of it. 1. There is a certain train or course of events that falls to every one of us, by the providence of God, during our life in this world. That is our lot, as being allotted to us by the sovereign God, our Creator and Governor, who holds in His hand our breath and all our ways. This train of events differs widely for different persons, according to the will and pleasure of the sovereign Manager, who orders men’s conditions in the world in great variety, some moving in a higher sphere, some in a lower. 2. In that train or course of events some fall out cross to us and against the grain, and these make the crook in our lot. While we are here, there will be cross events as well as agreeable ones in our lot and condition. Sometimes things are gliding on softly and agreeably, but by and by some incident alters that course, grates on us, and pains us, as when, having made a wrong step, we begin to limp. 3. Everybody’s lot in this world has some crook in it. Complainers are apt to make odious comparisons. They look about, and taking a distant view of the condition of others, can see nothing in it but what is straight and just as one would wish; so they pronounce their neighbor’s lot wholly straight. But that is a false verdict. There is no perfection here, no lot outside heaven without a crook. For of “all the things that are done under the sun,” “all is vanity and a pursuit of the wind. What is crooked cannot be made straight” (Eccl 1:14, 15). Who would not have thought Haman’s lot very straight, while his family was flourishing and he was prospering in riches and honor, the prime minister of state in the Persian court and high in the king’s favor? Yet at the same time there was a crook in his lot that so galled him that none of this satisfied him (Esth 5:13). Everyone feels for himself where he is pinched, though others do not see it. Nobody’s lot in this world is wholly crooked; there are always some straight and even parts in it. Indeed, when men’s passions have risen and cast a mist over their minds, they are ready to say that all is wrong with them and nothing right. But though in hell that tale is true, and ever will be, it is never true in this world. For there, indeed, not a drop of comfort is allowed (Luke 16:25), but here it always holds good that because of the loving devotion of the Lord we are not consumed (Lam 3:22). Lastly, the crook in the lot came into the world by sin; it is owing to the fall (Rom 5:12): “sin entered the world through one man, and death through sin.” Under that death the crook in the lot is included, just as a state of comfort or prosperity is expressed in the style of Scripture by living (1 Sam 25:6; John 4:50, 51). Sin so bent the hearts and minds of men that they became crooked with respect to the holy law, and God justly so bent their lot that it became crooked too. And this crook in our lot inseparably follows our sinful condition, until we drop this body of sin and death and get within heaven’s gates.

With these things set down first, a crook in the lot speaks in general of two things: (1.) adversity, (2.) continuance. Accordingly it makes a day of adversity, set against the day of prosperity in the verse right after the text.

The crook in the lot is, First, some piece or other of adversity. The prosperous part of one’s lot, which goes forward as one would wish, is its straight and even part; the adverse part, going the contrary way, is its crooked part. God has mixed these two together in men’s condition in this world, so that as there is some prosperity in it, making the straight line, there is also some adversity, making the crooked. This mixture has a place not only in the lot of the saints, who are told, “In the world you+ will have tribulation,” but even in the lot of all, as already observed. Secondly, it is adversity of some continuance. We do not count a thing crooked if, though forcibly bent and bowed together, it at once recovers its former straightness. There are twinges of the rod of adversity that pass like a stitch in one’s side, and all is immediately set right again. One’s lot may be suddenly clouded over, and the cloud vanish before he knows it. But under the crook a man has time to feel his pain, and is somewhat concerned to get the crook evened. So the crook in the lot is adversity continued for a shorter or longer time.

Now there is a threefold crook in the lot that befalls the children of men. (1.) There is one made by a cross dispensation which, however passing in itself, has lasting effects. Such a crook Herod’s cruelty made in the lot of the mothers in Bethlehem, who were left by the murderers weeping for their slain children and “refusing to be comforted, because they are no more” (Matt 2:18). A slip of the foot may soon be made that will make a man go limping all his life after. “Like fish caught in a cruel net … so men are ensnared in an evil time” (Eccl 9:12). The thing may happen in a moment under which the person will go limping to the grave. (2.) There is a crook made by a train of cross dispensations, whether of the same kind or of different kinds, following hard one on another and leaving lasting effects behind them. So in the case of Job, while one messenger of evil tidings was still speaking, another came (Job 1:16, 17, 18). Cross events coming one on the neck of another, deep calling to deep, make a sore crook. In that case the person is like one who draws back his sliding foot from one unsteady piece of ground and sets it on another just as unsteady, which at once gives way under him too. Or he is like one who, traveling an unknown mountainous track, has with difficulty made his way over one mountain and expects to see the plain country; but instead, time after time, a new mountain comes into view to be crossed. This crook in Asaph’s lot almost made him give up all his religion, until he entered God’s sanctuary, where this mystery of providence was unriddled to him (Ps 73:13–17). Solomon observes that “there are righteous men who get what the actions of the wicked deserve” (Eccl 8:14), providence taking a run against them, as if they were to be run down for good and all. Whoever there may be whose life in no part of it gives them experience of this, Joseph surely did not miss it in his young days, nor Jacob in his middle years, nor Peter in his old age (John 21:18), nor our Savior in all his days. (3.) There is a crook made by one cross dispensation, with its lasting effects, coming in the place of another that has been removed. So when one crook is straightened, another is made in its place, and there is still a crook. Lack of children had long been the crook in Rachel’s lot (Gen 30:1). That was at length evened to her mind, but then she got another in its place, hard labor in giving birth (ch. 35:16). This world is a wilderness, in which we may indeed get our station changed, but the move will be from one station in the wilderness to another. When one part of the lot is evened, usually some other part of it will be crooked.

More particularly, the crook in the lot has in it four things of the nature of what is crooked.

First, Disagreeableness. A crooked thing is wayward; laid against a rule, it does not answer to it but turns aside from it. In nobody’s lot is there any such thing as a crook with respect to the will and purpose of God. Take the harshest and most dismal dispensation in one’s lot and lay it against the eternal decree, made in the depths of infinite wisdom before the world began, and it will answer to it exactly, without the least deviation, everything being worked out by the counsel of His will (Eph 1:11). Lay it against the providential will of God in the government of the world, and there is perfect harmony. If Paul is to be bound at Jerusalem and handed over to the Gentiles, it is the Lord’s will that it should be so (Acts 21:11, 14). So the greatest crook of the lot on earth is straight in heaven; there is no disagreeableness in it there. But in everybody’s lot there is a crook with respect to their mind and natural inclination. The adverse dispensation lies cross to that rule, and will by no means answer to it or harmonize with it. When divine providence lays the one against the other, there is a plain disagreeableness: the man’s will goes one way and the dispensation another; the will bends upward, the cross events press down; so they are contrary. And there, and only there, lies the crook. It is this disagreeableness that makes the crook in the lot fit matter of exercise and trial for us in this our state of probation. In it, if you want to prove yourself approved to God, walking by faith and not by sight, you must quiet yourself in the will and purpose of God, and not insist that it should be according to your mind (Job 34:33).

Secondly, Unsightliness. Crooked things are unpleasant to the eye, and no crook in the lot seems enjoyable at the time, but painful; it makes only an unsightly appearance (Heb 12:11). Therefore men need to beware of letting their thoughts dwell on the crook in their lot, and of keeping it too much in view. David shows a hurtful experience of his own of that kind (Ps 39:3): “As I mused, the fire burned.” Jacob acted more wisely. He called his youngest son Benjamin, the son of the right hand, whom his dying mother had named Ben-oni, the son of my sorrow. By this means he made sure that the crook in his lot would not be set afresh before his eyes every time his son’s name was mentioned. Indeed, a Christian may safely take a steady and leisurely view of the crook in his lot in the light of the holy word, which represents it as the discipline of the covenant. In this way faith will find a hidden comeliness in it under a very unsightly outward appearance, perceiving how it suits the infinite goodness, love, and wisdom of God, and the real and most valuable interest of the person concerned. By this means a man comes to take pleasure, and that a most refined pleasure, in distresses (2 Cor 12:10). But whatever the crook in the lot may be to the eye of faith, it is not at all pleasant to sight.

Thirdly, Unfitness for motion. Solomon observes the cause of the uneasy and ungainly walking of the lame (Prov 26:7): “The legs of the lame are not equal.” Those who are exercised with the crook in their lot find this uneasiness: a high spirit and a low, adverse lot make great difficulty in the Christian walk. Nothing gives temptation easier access than the crook in the lot; nothing is more apt to occasion steps out of the way. Therefore the apostle says (Heb 12:13), “Make straight paths for your+ feet, so that what is lame may not be turned out of the way.” Those who are laboring under it, then, are to be pitied and not harshly censured, though they are rare persons who learn this lesson until taught by their own experience. It is long since Job made an observation on this case that holds good to this day (Job 12:5): “The one at ease scorns misfortune as the fate of those whose feet are slipping.”

Lastly, Aptness to catch hold and entangle, as with fishhooks (Amos 4:2). The crook in the lot so very readily makes an impression, ruffling and fretting one’s spirit and stirring up corruption, that Satan does not fail to make diligent use of it for these dangerous purposes. Once the tempter has gained that point, the tempted man, before he knows it, finds himself entangled as in a thicket, out of which he does not know how to free himself. In that temptation it often proves like a crooked stick stirring a standing pool, which not only raises up the mud all over it but brings up from the bottom some very ugly thing. So it brought up a touch of blasphemy and atheism in Asaph’s case (Ps 73:13): “Surely in vain I have kept my heart pure; in innocence I have washed my hands.” It is as if he had said: There is nothing at all in religion; it is a vain and empty thing that profits nothing; I was a fool to have been careful about purity and holiness, whether of heart or life. Ah! Is this the godly Asaph? How has he turned so wholly unlike himself! But the crook in the lot is a handle by which the tempter brings hidden corruption to light in surprising ways, even in the best.

This is the nature of the crook in the lot. Let us now observe in what part of the lot it falls.

And in general, three conclusions may be established on this head. First, it may fall in any part of the lot; no part is exempt in the case. For since sin is found in every part, the crook may take place in any part. Since we have all become like something unclean, we may all wither like a leaf (Isa 64:6). The main stream of sin, which the crook usually follows, runs in very different channels in different persons. And because of the various dispositions of men’s minds, what will prove a sinking weight to one, another would carry very lightly. Secondly, it may fall in many parts of the lot at once, the Lord summoning one’s terrors on every side, as for the day of an appointed feast (Lam 2:22). Sometimes God makes one notable crook in a man’s lot, but its name may be Gad, being only the forerunner of a troop that is coming. Then the crooks are multiplied, so that the person is made to limp on both sides. While one stream, let in from one quarter, is running full against him, another is let in on him from another quarter, until in the end the waters break in on every hand. Thirdly, it often falls in the tender part, I mean that part of the lot in which a man is least able to bear it, or at least thinks he is (Ps 55:12, 13): “It is not an enemy who insults me; that I could endure. … But it is you, a man like myself, my companion and close friend.” If there is any one part of the lot, above all others, in which a man is disposed to nestle, the thorn will usually be laid there, especially if he belongs to God. In the thing in which he can least of all bear to be touched, he will be sure to be pressed. There the trial of him will be taken, for there is the great competition with Christ: “I take away from them … the desire of their eyes, and that on which they set their minds” (Ezek 24:25). Since the crook in the lot is the special trial appointed for everyone, it is altogether reasonable, and worthy of the wisdom of God, that it should fall on that which, of all things, most rivals him.

But more particularly, the crook may be observed to fall in these four parts of the lot.

First, in the natural part, affecting persons considered in the make allotted them by the great God who formed all things. The parents of mankind, Adam and Eve, were formed wholly sound and entire, without the least blemish in soul or body. But in the forming of their descendants there often appears a notable variation from the original. Bodily defects, superfluities, deformities, and infirmities, natural or accidental, make the crook in the lot of some: they have something unsightly or grievous about them. Crooks of this kind, more or less noticeable, are very common and ordinary, and the best are not exempt from them; it is owing purely to sovereign pleasure that they are not more numerous. Weak eyes made the crook in Leah’s lot (Gen 29:17). Rachel’s beauty was balanced with barrenness, the crook in her lot (ch. 30:1). Paul, the great apostle of the Gentiles, was, it seems, no handsome man, but of a lowly outward appearance, for which fools were apt to despise him (2 Cor 10:10). Timothy had a frail constitution, weak and sickly (1 Tim 5:23). And there is a far more considerable crook still in the lot of the lame, the blind, the deaf, and the mute. Some are extremely weak in their intellect. And it is the crook in the lot of several bright souls to be overcast with clouds, notably dimmed and darkened by the frail bodies they are lodged in. We have an eminent instance of this in the grave, wise, and patient Job, going about mourning without the sun, yes, standing up in the assembly and crying out (Job 30:28).

Secondly, it may fall in the part of honor. There is an honor due to all men, the small as well as the great (1 Pet 2:17), and that on the ground of the original constitution of human nature, as it was framed in the image of God. But in the sovereign disposal of holy providence, the crook in the lot of some falls here. They are neglected and slighted; their standing is always kept low; they go through the world under a cloud, given a bad name, their reputation sunk. Sometimes this is the natural consequence of their own foolish and sinful conduct, as in the case of Dinah. By her gadding about to satisfy her youthful curiosity, regardless of a providential call and therefore not waiting for one, she brought a lasting stain on her honor (Gen 34). But where the Lord intends a crook of this kind in one’s lot, innocence will not be able to ward it off in an ill-natured world, nor will true merit be able to prevail against it, to make one’s lot stand straight in that part. So David represents his case (Ps 31:11, 12, 13): “… they flee when they see me on the street. I am forgotten like a dead man, out of mind. I am like a broken vessel. For I hear the slander of many.”

Thirdly, it may fall in the vocational part. Whatever men’s calling or station in the world, sacred or secular, the crook in their lot may take its place there. Isaiah was an eminent prophet, but most unsuccessful (Isa 53:1). Jeremiah met with such a train of discouragements and ill treatment in carrying out his sacred office that he very nearly gave it up, saying, “I will not mention Him or speak any more in His name” (Jer 20:9). The psalmist observes that this crook is often made in the lot of some men who are very industrious in their worldly business, who “sow fields,” and at times God “blesses them … He does not let their herds diminish”; but then again “they are decreased and humbled by oppression, evil, and sorrow” (Ps 107:37–39). Such a crook was made in Job’s lot, after it had long stood even. Some manage their work with all care and diligence: the farmer carefully laboring his ground; the sheep farmer “diligent to know the state of his flocks, and paying close attention to his herds”; the tradesman at his business early and late; the merchant diligently plying his, watching for and seizing the fairest and most promising opportunities. Yet there is such a crook in that part of their lot that all they are able to do can by no means even it. Why? The most proper means used to reach an end are of no effect without a word of divine appointment commanding their success: “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it?” (Lam 3:37). People ply their business with skill and industry, but the wind turns in their face. Providence crosses their undertakings, upsets their plans, frustrates their hopes and expectations, makes their efforts unsuccessful, and so puts them and keeps them in straitened circumstances. “The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise” (Eccl 9:11). Providence steps in and crooks the measures that human prudence and industry had laid straight toward their ends. So the swift lose the race, the strong the battle, and the wise miss their bread. Meanwhile some providential incident or other supplies what human wisdom, management, and ability lacked: the slow win the race and carry off the prize; the weak win the battle and enrich themselves with the spoil; and bread falls into the lap of the fool.

Lastly, it may fall in the relational part. Relationships are the joints of society, and there the crook in the lot may take its place, one’s sharpest pain often being felt in these joints. By their nature they are the springs of a man’s comfort, yet they often run with the greatest bitterness to him. Sometimes this crook is caused by the loss of relatives. So a crook was made in Jacob’s lot by the death of Rachel, his beloved wife, and the loss of Joseph, his son and darling, which almost made him go limping to the grave. Job laments this crook in his lot (Job 16:7): “You have devastated all my family,” meaning his dear children, every one of whom he had laid in the grave, not so much as one son or daughter left him. Again, sometimes it is made through the afflicting hand of God lying heavy on them, which, because of the relation, recoils on the person himself, as that believing woman feelingly expressed it (Matt 15:22): “Lord … have mercy on me! My daughter is miserably possessed by a demon.” Ephraim felt the pain of a course of family affliction when he named his son Beriah, because tragedy had come upon his house (1 Chr 7:23). Since all is not only vanity but vexation of spirit, it can hardly fail that the more of these springs of comfort are opened to a man, the more sources of sorrow he must find, at one time or another, to gush out and spring in on him; the sorrow is always in proportion to the comfort found in them or expected from them. And finally, the crook is sometimes made here by relations proving no comfort through the disagreeableness of their temper, disposition, and ways. There was a crook in Job’s lot through an undutiful, ill-natured wife (Job 19:17); in Abigail’s, through a surly, ill-tempered husband (1 Sam 25:25); in Eli’s, through the perverseness and obstinacy of his children (ch. 2:25); in Jonathan’s, through the furious temper of his father (ch. 20:30, 33). So men often find their greatest cross where they expected their greatest comfort. Sin has unhinged the whole creation and made every relation liable to the crook. In the family are found masters hard and unjust, and servants perverse and unfaithful; in the neighborhood, men selfish and hard to live with; in the church, ministers unedifying and offensive in their walk, and people contemptuous and disorderly, a burden to the spirits of ministers; in the state, magistrates oppressive and discouraging what is good, and subjects turbulent and seditious. All these cause crooks in the lot of those related to them.

And so much for the crook itself.

II. Having seen the crook itself, we are next to consider God’s making it. And here it is to be shown (1.) that it is of God’s making, (2.) how it is of his making, and (3.) why he makes it.

First, that the crook in the lot, whatever it is, is of God’s making appears from these three considerations.

First, it cannot be questioned that the crook in the lot, considered as the crook, is a penal evil, whatever it is in its matter. That is, whether the thing in itself, its immediate cause and occasion, is sinful or not, it is certainly a punishment or affliction. Now, as it may be brought on us as such, holily and justly, by our sovereign Lord and Judge, so he expressly claims the doing or making of it (Amos 3:6): “If evil comes to a city, has not the Lord done it?” So, since there can be no penal evil except of God’s making, and the crook in the lot is such an evil, it necessarily follows that it is of God’s making.

Secondly, it is evident from the scriptural doctrine of divine providence that God brings about every man’s lot and all its parts. He sits at the helm of human affairs and turns them wherever he pleases: “The Lord does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth, in the seas and in all their depths” (Ps 135:6). Nothing whatever befalls us without his overruling hand. The same providence that brought us out of the womb brings us to, and fixes us in, the condition and place allotted for us by him who has determined our appointed times and the boundaries of our dwelling (Acts 17:26). It overrules the smallest and most accidental things about us, such as the hairs of our head falling to the ground (Matt 10:29, 30), and the lot cast into the lap (Prov 16:33). Yes, it overrules the free acts of our will, by which we choose for ourselves, for even “the king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the Lord” (Prov 21:1). And it overrules all the steps we take, and those that others take with respect to us, for “a man’s way is not his own; no one who walks directs his own steps” (Jer 10:23). This holds whether the steps that cause the crook are deliberate and sinful ones, such as Joseph’s brothers selling him into Egypt, or undesigned ones, such as a purely accidental manslaughter, as when one cutting timber kills his neighbor with the blade flying off the handle (Deut 19:5). For there is a holy and wise providence that governs the sinful and the heedless actions of men, as a rider governs a lame horse: not the rider, but the horse’s own lameness, is the true and proper cause of its limping. That is why, in the first of these cases, God is said to have sent Joseph into Egypt (Gen 45:7), and in the second, to deliver one into his neighbor’s hand (Exod 21:13).

Lastly, God has, by an eternal decree immovable as mountains of bronze (Zech 6:1), appointed the whole of everyone’s lot, its crooked parts as well as its straight. By the same eternal decree by which the high and low parts of the earth, the mountains and the valleys, were appointed, the heights and depths, the prosperity and adversity, in the lot of its inhabitants are determined; and they are brought about in time in perfect agreement with it. The mystery of providence in the government of the world is, in all its parts, the building God rears up in exact conformity to the plan in his decree, he “who works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Eph 1:11). So there is never a crook in one’s lot that cannot be traced up to this source. Job sets us a godly example of this in his own case (Job 23:13, 14): “But He is unchangeable, and who can oppose Him? He does what He desires. For He carries out what He has appointed for me, and He has many such plans.”

Secondly, that we may see how the crook in the lot is of God’s making, we must distinguish between pure, sinless crooks and impure, sinful ones.

First, there are pure and sinless crooks. These are nothing but afflictions, clean crosses; grievous indeed, but not defiling. Such were Lazarus’s poverty, Rachel’s barrenness, Leah’s weak eyes, and the blindness of the man who had been blind from his birth (John 9:1). Now crooks of this kind are of God’s making by the efficacy of his power directly bringing them to pass and causing them to be. He is the maker of the poor (Prov 17:5): “He who mocks the poor insults their Maker”; that is, he insults God, who made them poor, according to 1 Sam 2:7: “The Lord makes poor.” It is he who holds the key of the womb, and as he sees fit shuts it (1 Sam 1:5) or opens it (Gen 29:31). And it is He who formed the eye (Ps 94:9). And the man was born blind so that the works of God would be displayed in him (John 9:3). So he says to Moses (Exod 4:11), “Who makes the mute or the deaf, the sighted or the blind? Is it not I, the Lord?” Such crooks in the lot are of God’s making in the fullest sense and in their whole extent, being the direct effects of his agency, just as the heavens and the earth are.

Secondly, there are impure, sinful crooks, which in their own nature are sins as well as afflictions, defiling as well as grievous. Such was the crook made in David’s lot through his family disorders: the defiling of Tamar, the murder of Amnon, the rebellion of Absalom, all of them unnatural. Of the same kind was the crook made in Job’s lot by the Sabeans and Chaldeans taking away his goods and killing his servants. As these were the afflictions of David and of Job respectively, so they were the sins of those who did them, the unhappy instruments of them. So one and the same thing may be to one man a heinous sin, defiling him and laying him under guilt, and to another an affliction, laying him under suffering only. Now crooks of this kind are not of God’s making in the same breadth of sense as those of the first kind. For he neither puts evil in anyone’s heart nor stirs anyone up to it: “God cannot be tempted by evil, nor does He tempt anyone” (Jas 1:13). But they are of his making by his holy permission of them, his powerful bounding of them, and his wise overruling of them to some good end.

First, he holily permits them, letting men go their own way (Acts 14:16). He is not the author of these sinful crooks; he does not cause them to be by the efficacy of his power. Yet if he did not permit them, willing not to hinder them, they could not be at all; for what He shuts no one can open (Rev 3:7). But he justly withholds his grace, which the sinner does not desire; he takes off the restraint under which the sinner is uneasy; and since the sinner will be gone, he lays the reins on his neck and leaves him to the free course of his lust. “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” (Hos 4:17). “Israel would not obey Me. So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts” (Ps 81:11, 12). In that unhappy situation the sinful crook follows naturally and unfailingly from the sinner’s own impulse, just as water runs down a hill wherever a gap is left open before it. So in these circumstances Israel went on “to follow their own devices” (v. 12). And in this way this kind of crook is of God’s making as a just Judge, punishing the sufferer by it. This view of the matter silenced David under Shimei’s cursing (2 Sam 16:11): “Leave him alone and let him curse me, for the Lord has told him so.”

Secondly, he powerfully bounds them (Ps 76:10): “The remainder of wrath” (that is, the creature’s wrath) “You will restrain.” If God did not set bounds to these crooks, however sore they are in anyone’s case, they would be sorer still. But he says to the sinful instrument, as he said to the sea, “You may come this far, but no farther; here your proud waves must stop.” He lays a restraining band on him, so that he cannot go one step farther in the way his headlong lust drives him than God sees fit to permit. So it comes about that a crook of this kind is neither more nor less, but just as great as God by his powerful bounding makes it to be. We have an eminent instance of this in the case of Job, whose lot was made crooked through a particular agency of the devil. But even to that great sinner God set a bound in the case: “The Lord said to Satan, ‘Everything he has is in your hands, but you must not lay a hand on the man himself’” (Job 1:12). Now Satan went the full length of the bound, leaving nothing within its compass untouched that he saw could serve his purpose (vv. 18, 19). But he could by no means move one step beyond it, to carry the point he could not gain within it. So to make the trial greater and the crook sorer, nothing remained but that the bound should be removed and the sphere of his agency enlarged. For this reason he says, “But stretch out Your hand and strike his flesh and bones, and he will surely curse You to Your face” (ch. 2:5). The bound was removed accordingly, but a new one was set at the same time (v. 6): “He is in your hands, but you must spare his life.” Then the crook was carried to the utmost the new bound would permit, consistent with Satan’s design of bringing Job to blaspheme: “Satan … infected Job with terrible boils from the soles of his feet to the crown of his head” (v. 7). And had it not been for this bound securing Job’s life, Satan, after finding this attempt unsuccessful too, would no doubt have finished him off for good and all.

Thirdly, he wisely overrules them to some good purpose worthy of the divine perfections. While the sinful instrument has an evil design in the crook he causes, God directs it to a holy and good end. In the disorders of David’s family, Amnon’s design was to gratify a brutish lust, and Absalom’s to glut himself with revenge and to satisfy his pride and ambition; but God meant by them to punish David for his sin in the matter of Uriah. In the crook made in Job’s lot by Satan and his instruments the Sabeans and Chaldeans, Satan’s design was to make Job blaspheme, and theirs to gratify their covetousness; but God had another design in it, worthy of himself, namely, to show Job’s sincerity and uprightness. If he did not wisely and powerfully overrule these crooks made in men’s lot, no good could come out of them. But he always overrules them so as to fulfill his own holy purposes by them, though the sinner does not intend it so; for his designs cannot miscarry: His purpose will stand (Isa 46:10). So the sinful crook is, by the overruling hand of God, turned about to his own glory and his people’s good in the end, according to the word: “The Lord has made all things for Himself” (Prov 16:4); “God works all things together for the good of those who love Him” (Rom 8:28). So Haman’s plot for the destruction of the Jews was overturned (Esth 9:1). And the crook made in Joseph’s lot by his own brothers selling him into Egypt was, on their part, most sinful and of a most malicious design. Yet, as it was of God’s making by his holy permission, powerful bounding, and wise overruling of it, it had an outcome well worthy of the divine wisdom and goodness. Joseph points out both to them (Gen 50:20): “As for you+, what you+ intended against me for evil, God intended for good, in order to accomplish a day like this—to preserve the lives of many people.”

Thirdly, it remains to inquire why God makes a crook in one’s lot. This is to be made clear by showing the design of that dispensation, a matter that concerns everyone to know and carefully to notice, in order to make a Christian use of the crook in their lot. The design of it seems to be chiefly sevenfold.

First, the trial of one’s state: whether one is in the state of grace or not; whether a sincere Christian or a hypocrite. Though every affliction is trying, yet here, I think, lies the main trial in providence that a man is put to with respect to his state. For the crook in the lot is a matter of continued course, so one has occasion to open and show himself again and again in the same thing. That is how it comes to give ground for a decision on that momentous point. It was plainly on this footing that the trial of Job’s state was put. The question was whether Job was an upright and sincere servant of God, as God himself testified of him, or only a mercenary one, a hypocrite, as Satan alleged against him. And the trial of this was put on the crook to be made in his lot (Job 1:8–12; 2:3–6). Accordingly, what all his friends except Elihu, the last speaker, aimed at in their reasoning with him under his trial was to prove him a hypocrite; so Satan made use of these good men to gain his point. God tested Israel in the wilderness for the land of Canaan by a train of afflicting dispensations. Caleb and Joshua bore them resolutely and were declared fit to enter the promised land, as men who had followed the Lord fully, while the others were worn out by them, and their bodies fell in the wilderness. In the same way God tests men for heaven by the crook in their lot. If one can stand that test, he is shown to be a saint, a sincere servant of God, as Job was proven to be. If not, he is only a hypocrite: he cannot stand the test of the crook in his lot, but goes away like dross in God’s furnace. We have a sad instance of this in that man of honor and wealth who came to our Savior with high pretensions to religion, arising from a principle of moral seriousness, to learn “what he must do to inherit eternal life” (Mark 10:17, 21). To show the man to himself, our Savior makes a crook in his lot, where all along before it had stood even. He binds him by a testing command to sell and give away all he had and follow him (v. 21): “Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor … Then come, take up the cross, and follow Me.” By this he was, at that moment, in the court of conscience, stripped of his great possessions, so that from then on he could no longer keep them with a good conscience, as he might have done before. The man instantly felt the sting of this crook made in his lot: “he was saddened by these words” (v. 22). That is, immediately on hearing it, he was struck with pain, disorder, and confusion of mind, and his countenance changed and became cloudy and overcast, as the same word is used in Matt 16:3. He could not stand the test of that crook. He could by no means submit his lot to God on that point, but must have it, at any cost, according to his own mind. So he “went away in sorrow, because he had great possessions.” He went away from Christ back to his plentiful estate, and though with a pained and sorrowful heart, he sat down on it again, a violent possessor before the Lord, thwarting the divine order. And there is no sign that this order was ever revoked, or that he ever came to a better temper about it.

Secondly, stirring up to duty: weaning one from this world and prompting him to look after the happiness of the other world. Many have the crook in their lot to thank that they ever came to themselves, settled down, and turned serious. For a time they went like a wild donkey at home in the wilderness, scorning to be turned. But their foot has slipped in due time, and a crook being made in their lot by it, their month has come, in which they have been caught (Jer 2:24). So the prodigal was brought to his senses and made to think of returning to his Father (Luke 15:17). The crook in their lot convinces them at length that their rest is not here. Whenever they lay down their head where they would most gladly take rest in created things, they still find a pricking thorn of uneasiness, and they are forced to lift their head again. So they are brought to conclude that there is no hope from that quarter, and they begin to look about for rest another way. In this way it gives them errands to God that they did not have before; for they feel a need of the comforts of the other world, for which they had lost their taste while their lot stood even to their liking. So whatever use we make of the crook in our lot, its voice is: “Arise and depart, for this is not your+ place of rest.” And surely, of all the means of mortification of the afflicting kind, it is the one that most deadens a real Christian to this life and world.

Thirdly, conviction of sin. When one walking carelessly is suddenly taken with a lameness, his limping the rest of his way convinces him that he has made a wrong step, and every new painful step brings it afresh to his mind. In the same way God makes a crook in one’s lot to convince him of some false step he has made, or some course he has taken. What the sinner would otherwise be apt to overlook, forget, or think lightly of is by this means recalled to mind, set before him as an evil and bitter thing, and kept in remembrance, so that his heart may bleed for it afresh every now and then. So by the crook men’s sin finds them out and convicts them, as the thief is ashamed when he is found (Num 32:23; Jer 2:26). Joseph’s brothers express this with feeling under the crook made in their lot in Egypt: “Surely we are guilty concerning our brother” (Gen 42:21); “God has found out the iniquity of your servants” (Gen 44:16). The crook in the lot usually, in its nature or circumstances, points so naturally back to the false step or course that it serves as a memorial of it in providence, bringing the sin fresh to remembrance, though it is of old date. It serves also as a badge of the sinner’s folly, in word or deed, to keep it always before him. When Jacob found Leah passed off on him for Rachel through Laban’s unfair dealing, how could he escape a stinging remembrance of the trick he had played on his own father at least seven years before, pretending to be Esau (Gen 27:19)? How could it fail to gall him at times afterward, through the course of the marriage? He had imposed the younger brother on his father for the elder, and Laban imposed the elder sister on him for the younger. The dimness of Isaac’s eyes favored the first trick, and the darkness of the evening favored the second just as much. So he had to say, as Adoni-bezek did in another case (Judg 1:7), “As I have done, so God has repaid me.” In the same way Rachel, dying in childbirth, could hardly avoid a sad reflection on her rash and passionate words recorded in Gen 30:1: “Give me children, or I will die.” Even holy Job read in the crook of his lot some false steps he had made in his youth many years before (Job 13:26): “You record bitter accusations against me and bequeath to me the iniquities of my youth.”

Fourthly, correction or punishment for sin. In nothing is that word more fully borne out than in the crook of the lot (Jer 2:19): “Your own evil will correct you.” God may for a time overlook one’s sin, on which he will afterward set a brand of his indignation by crooking the sinner’s lot, as he did in the case of Jacob and of Rachel, mentioned before. Though the sin was a passing action, or a course of no long continuance, the mark of the divine displeasure for it, set on the sinner in the crook of his lot, may pain him long and sorely, so that by repeated experience he may know what an evil and bitter thing it was. David’s killing of Uriah by the sword of the Ammonites was soon over, but for that cause the sword never departed from his house (2 Sam 12:10). Gehazi quickly got two bags of money from Naaman by falsehood and lying. But as a lasting mark of the divine indignation against that profane trick, he got along with it a leprosy that clung to him as long as he lived, and to his descendants after him (2 Kgs 5:27). This may be the case where the sin is pardoned, as to the guilt of eternal wrath, as well as where it is not. One may have confessed and sincerely repented of a sin that will still make him go limping to the grave, though it cannot carry him to hell. A man’s person may be accepted in the Beloved, and yet he may have a particular badge of the divine displeasure with his sin hung on him in the crook of his lot (Ps 99:8): “You were a forgiving God to them, yet an avenger of their misdeeds.”

Fifthly, preventing of sin (Hos 2:6): “I will hedge up her path with thorns; I will enclose her with a wall, so she cannot find her way.” The crook in the lot will usually be found to lie across some wrong bias of the heart that has a special sway with the person. So it is like a thorn hedge or a wall in the way that bias inclines him to take. The defiling objects in the world especially attract and ensnare men as they suit the particular cast of each man’s temper. But by means of the crook in the lot the paint and varnish are worn off the defiling object, and it loses its former attractive look. So, the fuel being removed, the edge of corrupt affections is blunted, temptation is weakened, and much sin is prevented. The sinner, after gadding about so much to change his way, returns ashamed (Jer 2:36–37). So the Lord crooks one’s lot “to turn a man from wrongdoing and keep him from pride,” and so “to preserve his soul from the Pit” (Job 33:17–18). Everyone knows what is most pleasing to him, but God alone knows what is most profitable. As all men are liars, so all men are fools too; he is the only wise God (Jude 25). Many owe it to the crook in their lot that they do not run into those excesses to which their vain minds and corrupt affections would carry them under full sail. And they would bless God from their hearts for making it, if they would only calmly consider what the outcome of its removal would most likely be. When one is in danger of fretting under the hardship of bearing the crook, he would do well to consider what condition he is yet in to bear its removal in a Christian manner.

Sixthly, discovery of hidden corruption, whether in saints or sinners. There are some corruptions in every man’s heart that lie, as it were, so near the surface that they are ready to come up at every turn. But there are others that lie so very deep that they are scarcely noticed at all. As the fire under the pot makes the scum rise, appear on top, and run over, so the crook in the lot stirs up from the bottom and brings out such corruption as one would hardly otherwise imagine to be within. Who would have suspected such strength of anger in the meek Moses as he showed at the waters of strife, for which he was kept out of Canaan (Ps 106:32–33; Num 20:13)? Or so much bitterness of spirit in the patient Job, that he charged God with becoming cruel to him (Job 30:21)? Or so much ill nature in the good Jeremiah, that he cursed not only the day of his birth, but even the man who brought the news of it to his father (Jer 20:14–15)? Or such a tang of atheism in Asaph, that he pronounced religion a vain thing (Ps 73:13)? But the crook in the lot, bringing these things out, showed that they had been within, however long they had lurked unobserved. This design, however unbecomingly proud scoffers allow themselves to treat it, is in no way inconsistent with the divine perfections. And the discovery itself is necessary for the due humiliation of sinners, and to stain the pride of all glory, so that men may know themselves. Both of these appear in this: it was for this very design that God made the long-continued crook in Israel’s lot in the wilderness, namely, to humble them and test them, to know what was in their heart (Deut 8:2).

Lastly, the exercise of grace in the children of God. Through the remains of indwelling corruption, believers are liable to fits of spiritual laziness and inactivity, in which their graces lie dormant for the time. Besides, there are some graces that by their own nature are exercised only on occasion, that is, only on the occasion of certain things to which they have a necessary relation, such as patience and long-suffering. Now the crook in the lot serves to rouse a Christian to exercise the graces that corruption has overpowered, and also to call the occasional graces into action by giving them proper occasions. The truth is, the crook in the lot is the great engine of providence for making men appear in their true colors, showing both their evil and their good. If the grace of God is in them, it will bring it out and make it display itself. It so drives the Christian to his last resources that, however it makes him stagger for a while, it will at length give evidence of both the reality and the strength of grace in him: “You+ … suffer grief in various trials, so that the trial of your+ faith, more precious than gold, which perishes … may result in praise” (1 Pet 1:6–7). The crook in the lot gives rise to many acts of faith, hope, love, self-denial, resignation, and other graces, and to many heavenly breathings, pantings, longings, and groanings that would not otherwise be brought forth. And I have no doubt that these things, however carnal men despise them as trifling, are more precious in the sight of God than even believers themselves are aware, being acts of immediate inward worship. They will have a surprising notice taken of them, and of the sum of them, in the long run, however little the persons themselves can think them worth their own notice at all. We know who has said to the gracious soul, “Let me see your face … your countenance is lovely” (Song 2:14), and “You have stolen my heart with one glance of your eyes” (Song 4:9). The steady action of a gallant army of horsemen and foot soldiers in defeating the enemy is highly prized. But the action of holy fear and humble hope is in reality far more valuable, since it is so in the sight of God, whose judgment, we are sure, is according to truth. The psalmist teaches this (Ps 147:10, 11): “He does not delight in the strength of the horse; He takes no pleasure in the legpower of the man. The Lord is pleased with those who fear Him, who hope in His loving devotion.” And indeed the exercise of the graces of his Spirit in his people is so very precious in his sight that, whatever grace any of them excel in, they will likely get such a crook made in their lot as will be a special trial for it, one that will make a proof of its full strength. Abraham excelled in the grace of faith, in trusting God’s bare word of promise in spite of what he could see. God gave him a promise that he would make of him a great nation, and with it made a crook in his lot with which he had all he could do, with all the strength of his faith. He was required to leave his country and his kindred for good and all, and to live as a stranger among the Canaanites. His wife remained barren until past the age of childbearing. And when she had at length given birth to Isaac, and he had grown up, Abraham was called to offer him up as a burnt offering. It was all the sharper a trial of his faith because Ishmael had now been sent out of his family, and it had been declared that in Isaac only his offspring should be called (Gen 21:12). “Moses was a very meek man, more so than any man on the face of the earth” (Num 12:3). And he was entrusted with leading a most perverse and unmanageable people, the crook in his lot plainly designed for the exercise of his meekness. Job excelled in patience, and by the crook in his lot he had just as much use for it. For God gives none of his people to excel in a gift but, at one time or another, he will give them use for the whole compass of it.

Now the use of this doctrine is threefold: (1.) for reproof; (2.) for consolation; and (3.) for exhortation.

Use 1. Of reproof. It falls on three sorts of persons as deserving reproof.

First, the carnal and earthly, who do not regard the crook in their lot with awe and reverence as of God’s making. There is certainly a signature of the divine hand on it, to be seen by those who observe rightly. That calls for a regard full of awe, and the neglect of it forebodes destruction (Ps 28:5): “Since they show no regard for the works of the Lord or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them.” Here they are deeply guilty who pore over second causes and look no further than the unhappy instruments of the crook in their lot, and so overlook the first cause, as a dog snarls at the stone but does not look to the hand that threw it. This is in effect to make a god of a created thing, regarding it as if it could bring about anything of itself, while in the meantime it is only an instrument in the hand of God, the rod of his anger (Isa 10:5), appointed by him for judgment, established for correction (Hab 1:12). Oh, why should men stop their view at the instruments of the crook in their lot, and so magnify their scourges? The truth is, they are for the most part rather to be pitied, as having an undesirable office. Because they gratify their own corrupt affections in making the crook in the lot of others, that office comes back at length on their own heads with a vengeance, as did the blood of Jezreel on the house of Jehu (Hos 1:4). And it is especially undesirable to be so employed in the case of those who belong to God. For the ground of the quarrel is rarely the same on the instrument’s part as on God’s part, but very different. Witness Shimei’s cursing David as a man of bloodshed, meaning the blood of the house of Saul, of which David was not guilty, while God meant it of the blood of Uriah, which David could not deny (2 Sam 16:7–8). Moreover, in the long run the quarrel between God and his people will be made up, and then their scourges will find they had only a thankless office (Zech 1:15). “I was a little angry, but they have added to the calamity,” says God, resenting the heathen nations’ crooking the lot of his people. In the same way they are guilty who put the crook in their lot down to fortune, or their bad luck, which in very truth is nothing but a creature of imagination, framed as a blind to keep men from acknowledging the hand of God. So what the Philistines were unsure of, these people most impiously settle, saying in effect, “It was not His hand that punished us; it happened by chance” (1 Sam 6:9). And finally, those are guilty too who give themselves up to carnal mirth and sensuality, and so set themselves to despise the crook in their lot, to make nothing of it, and to forget it. I do not question that one who commits his case to the Lord, and looks to him for remedy in the first place, may lawfully call in the moderate use of the comforts of life for help in the second place. But as for that course, so frequent and usual in this case among carnal men: if the crook of the lot really is of God’s making, as indeed it is, it must be a most unfitting and unbecoming course, to be abhorred by all good men (Prov 3:11): “My son, do not despise the discipline of the Lord.” It is surely a very desperate method of cure, which cannot fail to end in something worse than the disease, however it may ease it for a while (Isa 22:12–14): “On that day the Lord God of Hosts called for weeping and wailing … But look, there is joy and gladness … eating of meat and drinking of wine … The Lord of Hosts has revealed in my hearing: ‘Until your+ dying day, this sin of yours+ will never be atoned for.’”

Secondly, the unsubmissive, whose hearts, like the troubled sea, swell and boil, fret and grumble, and cannot be at rest under the crook in their lot. This is a most sinful and dangerous course. The apostle Jude, describing some for whom blackest darkness has been reserved forever (v. 13), says of them in verse 16, “These men are grumblers, complainers,” that is, always complaining of their lot, which is the meaning of the word the Holy Spirit uses there. For since the crook in their lot, to which their unsubdued spirits can by no means submit, is of God’s making, this practice of theirs must be a fighting against God, and their complaining and grumbling is really against him, whatever face they put on it. So when the Israelites grumbled against Moses (Num 14:2), God charges them with grumbling against himself: “How long will this wicked congregation grumble against Me?” (v. 27). Ah! May not he who made and fashioned us without our advice be allowed to make our lot too without asking our mind, but we must rise up against him because of the crook made in it? What does this say, but that the proud creature cannot endure God’s work, nor digest what he has done? And how black and dangerous is that temper of spirit! How is it possible to escape being broken to pieces in such a course? “God is wise in heart and mighty in strength. Who has resisted Him and prospered?” (Job 9:4).

Lastly, the careless and unfruitful, who do not set themselves dutifully to comply with the design of the crook in their lot. God and nature do nothing in vain. Since he makes the crook, there is no doubt a fitting design in it, which we are bound in duty to fall in with, according to Mic 6:9: “Heed the rod.” And indeed, if one does not shut his own eyes but is willing to understand, he may easily see that its general design is to wean him from this world and move him to seek and take up his heart’s rest in God. And if the nature and circumstances of the crook itself are duly considered, it will not be very hard to find out its design more particularly. But alas! The careless sinner, sunk in spiritual sloth and stupidity, has no concern to discover the design of providence in the crook. So he cannot fall in with it, but remains unfruitful, and all the pains the great Vinedresser takes with him in the dispensation are lost. “They cry out for relief from the arm of the mighty,” groaning under the pressure of the crook itself and the weight of the hand of its instrument, “but no one asks, ‘Where is God my Maker?’” They do not look, they do not turn to God for all that (Job 35:9–10).

Use II. Of consolation. It speaks comfort to the afflicted children of God. Whatever the crook in your+ lot is, it is of God’s making, and therefore you+ may look on it kindly. Since it is your+ Father who has made it for you+, do not doubt that there is a favorable design in it toward you+. A wise child welcomes his father’s rod, knowing that, being a father, he seeks his good by it. And shall not God’s children welcome the crook in their lot as designed by their Father, who cannot mistake his measures in working for their good, according to the promise? The truth is, the crook in the lot of a believer, however painful it proves, is a part of the discipline of the covenant, the nurture secured to Christ’s children by the promise of the Father (Ps 89:30, 32): “If his children forsake My law and do not walk in My judgments … I will attend to their transgression with the rod.” Further, all who are disposed to betake themselves to God under the crook in their lot may take comfort in this. Let them know that there is no crook in their lot that cannot be made straight: for God made it, so surely he can mend it. He himself can make straight what he has made crooked, though no one else can. There is nothing too hard for him to do: “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the dump to seat them with nobles … He settles the barren woman in her home as a joyful mother to her children” (Ps 113:7–9). Do not say that your+ crook has lasted so long that it will never mend. Put it in the hand of God, who made it, so that he may mend it, and wait on him. And if it is for your good that it should be mended, it will be mended; for “He withholds no good thing from those who walk with integrity” (Ps 84:11).

Use last, of exhortation. Since the crook in the lot is of God’s making, then, eyeing the hand of God in yours+, be reconciled to it, and submit under it, whatever it is. I say, eyeing the hand of God in it, for otherwise your+ submission under the crook in your+ lot cannot be a Christian submission, acceptable to God, since it has no reference to him as the party you+ have to deal with in the matter.

Object. I. But some will say, The crook in my lot is from the hand of man, and from one, too, from whom I deserved no such treatment. Answer. From what has already been said it appears that, although the crook in your lot comes directly from man’s hand, yet through man it comes from the hand of God. For there is nothing of that kind, no penal evil, but the Lord has done it. Therefore, beyond all doubt, God himself is the principal party you have to deal with, whoever the lesser one may be. And although you have not deserved your crook at the hand of the instrument or instruments he uses for your correction, you certainly deserve it at his hand. And he may use whatever instrument he pleases in the matter, or may do it directly by himself, just as seems good in his sight.

Object. 2. But the crook in my lot might quickly be evened, if the instrument or instruments of it pleased; only, there is no dealing with them so as to convince them of their fault in making it. Answer. If that is so, you may be sure that God’s time has not yet come for that crook to be evened. For if it had come, though they now stand like an impregnable fort, they would give way like a sandy bank under one’s feet; they would “bow to you facedown and lick the dust at your feet” (Isa 49:23). Meanwhile, that state of the matter is so far from justifying one’s not eyeing the hand of God in the crook in the lot that it is itself a piece of trial in which his hand very plainly appears: namely, that men should be notably injurious and burdensome to others, and yet by no means open to conviction. This was the trial of the church from her adversaries (Jer 50:7): “All who found them devoured them, and their enemies said, ‘We are not guilty, for they have sinned against the Lord, the habitation of justice.’” They were very abusive and treated her barbarously, yet they would admit no fault in the matter. How could they ward off the conviction? Were they truly blameless in devouring the Lord’s straying sheep? No, surely they were not. Did they look on themselves as ministers of divine justice against her? No, they did not. Some indeed would raise a question here: how could the adversaries of the church celebrate her God as the habitation of justice? But if the original pointing of the Hebrew text is kept, it appears that there is no ground at all for this question here, and at the same time the whole matter is set in a clear light: “All who found them devoured them; and their enemies said, ‘We are not guilty’; because they have sinned against the Lord, the habitation of justice.” These last are not the words of the adversaries, but the words of the prophet. He is showing how it came about that the adversaries devoured the Lord’s sheep as they came upon them, and stood to the defense of it when they had done it, far from acknowledging any wrong. The matter lay here: the sheep had sinned against the Lord, the habitation of justice, and as a just punishment for this from his hand, they could have no justice at the hand of their adversaries.

Therefore, laying aside these trifling pretexts, and eyeing the hand of God as that which has bent your+ lot in that part and keeps it bent, be reconciled to the crook and submit under it, whatever it is, saying from the heart, “This is truly my grief, and I must bear it” (Jer 10:19).

And to move you+ to this, consider: (1.) It is a duty you+ owe to God as your+ sovereign Lord and Benefactor. His sovereignty claims our submission. It can in no case be baseness of spirit to submit to the crook that his hand has made in our lot, and to go quietly under the yoke that he has laid on us. But it is really madness for the potsherds of the earth to strive with their Maker by turbulent and stubborn behavior under it. And his goodness to us, ill-deserving creatures, may well stop our mouths from complaining of his making a crook in our lot, when he would have done us no wrong if he had made the whole of it crooked: “Should we accept from God only good and not adversity?” (Job 2:10). (2.) It is an unalterable statute, for the time of this life, that nobody shall be without a crook in their lot; for “man is born to trouble as surely as sparks fly upward” (Job 5:7). And those who are designed for heaven are assured in a special way of a crook in theirs, that in the world they will have tribulation (John 16:33); for by means of it the Lord makes them fit for heaven. And how can you+ imagine that you+ will be exempted from the common lot of mankind? “Should the rocks be moved from their place on your account?” And since God makes the crooks in men’s lot according to the different needs of their cases, you+ may be sure that yours+ is necessary for you+. (3.) A crook in the lot that one can by no means submit to makes a condition, of all things, the most like that in hell. For there a yoke that the wretched sufferers can neither bear nor shake off is wreathed about their necks. There the almighty arm draws against them, and they against it. There they are ever suffering and ever sinning, always in the furnace, yet their dross is not consumed, nor are they purified. Such is the case of those who now cannot submit under the crook in their lot. Lastly, great is the loss of not submitting under it. The crook in the lot, rightly used, has turned to the best account for some, and made the best time they ever had in all their lives, as the psalmist testifies from his own experience (Ps 119:67): “Before I was afflicted, I went astray; but now I keep Your word.” There are many now in heaven who are blessing God for the crook they had in their lot here. What a sad thing it must be, then, to lose this wind in our teeth on the way to Immanuel’s land! But if the crook in your lot does you no good, be sure it will not fail to do you great harm. It will hugely increase guilt and aggravate your condemnation, while it will forever cut you to the heart to think of the pains taken with you by means of the crook in the lot, to wean you from the world and bring you to God, but all in vain. Take heed, therefore, how you+ manage it, lest “at the end of your life you groan … and you say, ‘How I hated discipline, and my heart despised reproof!’” (Prov 5:11, 12).

Doctrine II.

What God sees fit to mar, we will not be able to mend in our lot. What crook God makes in our lot, we will not be able to even.

We shall, 1st, show God’s marring and making a crook in one’s lot, as he sees fit.

2dly, We shall consider men’s attempting to mend or even that crook in their lot.

3dly, In what sense it is to be understood that we will not be able to mend or even the crook in our lot.

4thly, Give some reasons for the point.

I. As to the first head, namely, etc.

1. God keeps the choice of every one’s crook to himself, and in this he exercises his sovereignty (Matt 20:15). It is not left to our choice what that crook shall be, or what our particular burden. But as the potter makes of the same clay one vessel for one use and another for another use, so God makes one crook for one and another for another, according to his will and pleasure (Ps 135:6): “The Lord does all that pleases Him in the heavens and on the earth,” etc.

2. He sees and observes the bias of everyone’s will and inclination, how it lies, and where it especially bends away from himself, and so where it needs the special bend. So he did in that man’s case (Mark 10:21): “There is one thing you lack: Go, sell everything you own and give to the poor,” etc. Observe the bent of his heart toward his great possessions. God takes notice what idol in each one’s case is most apt to be his rival, so that he may suit the trial to the case, making the crook there.

3. By the guidance of his providence, or a touch of his hand, he gives that part of one’s lot a bend the opposite way, so that from then on it lies quite contrary to that bias of the person’s will (Ezek 24:25). And here the trial is made: the bent of the will lies one way, and that part of one’s lot another, so that it does not answer to the person’s inclination but runs against it.

Lastly, he wills that crook in the lot to remain as long as he sees fit, for a longer or shorter time, just according to the holy ends of his own for which he designs it (2 Sam 12:10; Hos 5:15). By that will it is so fixed that the whole creation cannot alter it or take the bend out of it.

II. We shall consider men’s attempting to mend or even that crook in their lot. In a word, this lies in their making efforts to bring their lot on that point into line with their own will, so that the two may go one way. So it implies three things.

First, a certain uneasiness under the crook in the lot. It is a yoke that is hard for the person to bear until his spirit is tamed and subdued (Jer 31:18): “You disciplined me severely, like a calf unaccustomed to the yoke. Restore me, that I may return,” etc. And it is to break down the weight of one’s spirit that God lays it on. For this reason it is declared to be a good thing to bear it (Lam 3:27), since that is the way to make one at length like a weaned child.

Secondly, a strong desire to have the cross removed, and to have things on that point go according to our inclinations. This is very natural, for nature desires to be freed from everything that is burdensome or contrary to it. And if that desire is kept in due subordination to the will of God, and is not too peremptory, it is not sinful (Matt 26:39): “If it is possible, let this cup pass from Me. Yet not as I will,” etc. That is why so many prayers of the people of God for the removal of the crook in their lot have been accepted.

Lastly, an earnest use of means to that end. This follows naturally on that desire. The man, pressed with the cross that is his crook, labors all he can in the use of means to be rid of it. And if the means used are lawful, and are not relied on but followed with an eye to God in them, the attempt is not sinful either, whether he succeeds in the use of them or not.

III. In what sense is it to be understood that we will not be able to mend or even the crook in our lot?

Negatively, it is not to be understood as if the case were absolutely hopeless and there were no remedy for the crook in the lot. For there is no case so desperate but God may set it right (Gen 18:14): “Is anything too difficult for the Lord?” When the crook has continued long and has defied all the remedies one has used for it, one is ready to lose hope about it. But many a crook given up as hopeless, that would never mend, God has made perfectly straight, as in Job’s case. But,

Positively, we will never be able to mend it by ourselves. If the Lord himself does not take it in hand to remove it, it will stand before us immovable, like a mountain of bronze, though perhaps it may in itself be a thing that might easily be removed. We take this up in these three things.

1. It will never be done by the mere force of our hand (1 Sam 2:9): “… for by his own strength shall no man prevail.” The most vigorous efforts we can make will not even the crook if God does not give it a touch of his hand. So all efforts that way without an eye to God are vain and fruitless, and will be only plowing on the rock (Ps 127:1–2).

2. Nor by the use of all allowable means, for it will be unsuccessful unless the Lord blesses them for that end (Lam 3:37): “Who has spoken and it came to pass, unless the Lord has commanded it?” As one may eat and not be satisfied, so one may use proper means for making the crook even in his lot and yet achieve nothing. For nothing can be or do anything for us beyond what God makes it be or do (Eccl 9:11): “… The race is not to the swift, nor the battle to the strong; neither is the bread to the wise, nor the wealth to the intelligent,” etc.

3. It will never be done in our time, but in God’s time, which is seldom as early as ours (John 7:6): “Although your+ time is always at hand, My time has not yet come.” That is why the crook sometimes remains immovable, as if it were held by an invisible hand, and at another time goes away at a touch, because God’s time for making it even has come.

IV. Reasons for the point.

1st, Because of the absolute dependence we have on God (Acts 17:28). As the light depends on the sun, or the shadow on the body, so we depend on God, and without him can do nothing, great or small. And God will have us find it so, to teach us our dependence.

2dly, Because his will is irresistible (Isa 46:10): “My purpose will stand, and all My good pleasure I will accomplish.” When God wills one thing and a created being the opposite, it is easy to see which will must be done. When the almighty arm holds, every created thing pulls in vain (Job 9:4): “Who has resisted Him and prospered?”

Inference 1. There is a necessity of yielding and submitting under the crook in our lot. For we may as well think to remove the rocks and mountains that God has settled as to make that part of our lot straight which he has made crooked.

2. Evening the crook in our lot by main force of our own is only a cheat we put on ourselves, and it will not last. Like a stick made straight by main force, it will quickly return to its bend again.

Lastly, the only effectual way of getting the crook made even is to apply to God for it.

Exhortation 1. Let us then apply to God for the removal of any crook in our lot that may be removed in the settled order of things. Men can no more stop desiring the removal of a crook than the removal of a thorn in the flesh. But since we are not able to mend what God sees fit to mar, it is evident that we are to apply to him who made it to mend it, and not take the making of it even into our own hands.

Motive 1. Without him, all our attempts to remove it will be vain and fruitless (Ps 127:1). Let us be as determined as we like to have it made even; if God does not say so, we will labor in vain (Lam 3:37). However promising the means we use may look, they will be ineffectual if he does not command a blessing (Eccl 9:11).

2. Such attempts will likely make it worse. Nothing is more common than for a proud spirit, struggling with the crook, to make it more crooked (Eccl 10:8, 9): “he who breaches a wall may be bitten by a snake.” Verse 9: “The one who quarries stones may be injured by them,” and so on. This is evident in the case of the murmurers in the wilderness. It comes about naturally, because in that way the will of the person bends still farther away from it. And moreover, God is provoked to bind the yoke all the tighter about his neck, because the man will by no means let it sit easy on him.

3. There is no crook that may not be remedied by him and made perfectly straight (Ps 146:8): “The Lord lifts those who are bowed down,” and so on. He can raise up the oldest and most settled trouble, about which no hope remains with us (Rom 4:17): “who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not yet exist.” It is his prerogative to do wonders: to begin a work where the whole creation gives it up as hopeless, and to carry it on to perfection (Gen 18:14).

4. He loves to be employed in making crooks even, and calls us to employ him in that way (Ps 50:15): “Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you,” and so on. He makes them for that very end, that he may bring us to him on that errand, and may show his power and goodness in making them even (Hos 5:15). The straits of the children of men give a large field for displaying his glorious perfections, which would otherwise be lacking (Exod 15:11).

5. A crook made even in this way is a double mercy. Some crooks are made even by a touch of the hand of common providence, while people are either not spiritually exercised about them or are fretting for their removal. These are sapless and short-lived mercies (Ps 78:30, 31; Hos 13:11).
