Fruit plucked so hastily from the tree of providence can hardly fail to set the teeth on edge, and will certainly be bitter to gracious souls. But oh, how sweet is the making even of the crook obtained by humbly applying to the Lord and waiting on him! It bears the image and inscription of divine favor, which makes it weighty and valuable (Gen 33:10): “For indeed, I have seen your face, and it is like seeing the face of God,” and so on; and Gen 21:6.

6. God has shown his favor most notably to his dearest children in making and mending remarkable crooks in their lot. His darling ones ordinarily have the greatest crooks made in their lot (Heb 12:6). But then these make way for the richest experience in their removal, when his children apply to him. This is clear from the case of Abraham, Jacob and Joseph. Which of the patriarchs had such great crooks as they? But which of them, on the other hand, had such signal tokens of divine favor? The greatest of men, such as Samson and John the Baptist, were born of women naturally barren. In the same way, the greatest crooks issue in the richest mercies to those who are trained by them.

Lastly, it is the shortest and surest way to go straight to God with the crook in the lot. If we would have our wish in that matter, we must, like the eagle, first soar aloft and then come down on the prey (Mark 5:36). Our faithless, irregular attempts to make the crook even are our fool’s haste, which is no speed, as in the case of Abraham’s going in to Hagar. God is the first mover, who sets all the wheels in motion for making the crook even; without him it will remain immovable (Hos 2:21, 22).

Object. (1.) But it is needless. For I see that though the crook in my lot could be mended, yet it never will be. In its own nature it is capable of being removed, but it is plain that it is not to be removed; it is hopeless. Answer. That is the language of unbelieving haste, which faith and patience should correct (Ps 116:11, 12). Abraham had as much to say for the hopelessness of his crook, and yet he applied to God in faith for its mending (Rom 4:19, 20). Sarah had drawn such a conclusion, and she was rebuked for it (Gen 18:13, 14). Nothing can make it needless to apply to God in such a case.

Object. (2.) But I have applied to him for it again and again, yet it is never mended. Answer. Delays at the court of heaven are not denials of the petitions, but trials of the faith and patience of the petitioners. And whoever will hold on will certainly succeed in the long run (Luke 18:1, 7, 8): “Will not God bring about justice for His elect who cry out to Him day and night, though He bears long with them?” Verse 8: “I tell you+, He will promptly carry out justice on their behalf.” Sometimes indeed people grow peevish in the case of the crook in the lot, and in their despondency let it drop out of their prayers, while it still remains a trouble to them. But if God intends to make it even in mercy, he will make them take it back into their prayers (Ezek 36:37): “Once again I will be inquired of by the house of Israel, to do this for them,” and so on. If the removal comes while it is dropped from their prayers, there will be little substance in it. Even if it were never to be removed while we live, that should not cut off our applying to God for its removal. For there are many prayers that will not be answered until we come to the other world, and there all will be answered at once (Rom 7:24).

Directions for rightly managing the application for removing the crook in the lot.

1. Pray for it (Ezek 36:37), and pray in faith, believing that for the sake of Jesus you+ will certainly obtain it at length, and in this life too, if it is good for you+; but in the other life without any doubt (Matt 21:22). Those who get the song of Moses and of the Lamb will not be disappointed (Rev 15:3). And in some cases of that kind, extraordinary prayer with fasting is very fitting (Matt 17:21).

2. Humble yourselves+ under it, as the yoke that the sovereign hand has laid on you+ (Mic 7:9): “I will bear the rage of the Lord, because I have sinned against Him,” and so on. Justify God, condemn yourselves+, kiss the rod, and go quietly under it. This is the most promising way to be rid of it (Jas 4:10). When the bullock is broken and tamed, as being used to the yoke, then the yoke is taken off, its end being obtained (Ps 10:17): “You will prepare their hearts; You will incline Your ear.”

Lastly, wait patiently until the hand that made it mends it (Ps 27:14). Do not give the matter up as hopeless because you+ are not relieved as soon as you+ would like. Rather, “let patience finish its work, so that you+ may be mature and complete, not lacking anything” (Jas 1:4). Leave the timing of the deliverance to the Lord. His time will at length appear, to your+ full conviction, to be the best, and the deliverance will not go beyond it (Isa 60:22): “I am the Lord in its time I will accomplish it quickly.” Waiting on him, you+ will not be disappointed: “those who wait for Me will never be put to shame” (Isa 49:23).

Exhortation 2. Whatever crook there is that cannot be removed or made even in this world, in the settled order of things, let us apply to God for suitable relief under it. For instance, there is the common crook in the lot of the saints, namely, indwelling sin. As God has made that crook one not to be removed here, he can certainly balance it and give relief under it. The same is to be said of any crook while it remains unremoved. In both cases apply yourself to God to make up your losses another way. And there are five things I would have you keep in view and aim at here.

1. To take God in Christ for, and instead of, that thing whose withholding or taking away from you makes the crook in your lot (Ps 142:4, 5). God never makes a crook in our lot but it is in effect Heaven’s offer of a blessed exchange to us, such as that in Mark 10:21: “sell everything you own … and you will have treasure in heaven.” In managing this exchange, God first puts out his hand and takes some earthly thing away from us. And it is expected that we put out our hand next and take some heavenly thing from him in its place, and particularly his Christ. Why has God emptied his left hand of such and such an earthly comfort? Stretch out your right hand to God in Christ, take him in its place, and welcome. That is why the soul’s embracing Christ is called buying, in which, parting with one thing, we get another in its place (Matt 13:45, 46): “The kingdom of heaven is like a merchant in search of fine pearls.” Verse 46: “When he found one very precious pearl, he went away and sold all he had and bought it.” Do this, and you will more than come out even with the crook in your lot.

2. Look for the stream to run as full from him as ever it did or could run, when the crook of the lot has dried it up. This is the work of faith: confidently to hold on to God for what is denied us from created things. “Though my father and mother forsake me, the Lord will receive me” (Ps 27:10). This is a most reasonable expectation. For it is certain that there is no good in created things but what is from God. Therefore there is no good to be found in created things, the stream, but what may be had directly from God, the Fountain. And oh, what a welcome plea it is to come to God and say, “Now, Lord, you have taken away from me such an earthly comfort; I must have as good from yourself.”

3. The spiritual fruits of the crook in the lot (Heb 12:11). We see that the way in the world is, when one trade fails, to take up and drive another trade. So we, when there is a crook in the lot bringing our earthly comforts low, should set ourselves all the more to spiritual attainments. If our trade with the world sinks, let us see to driving a trade with heaven more vigorously. Let us see whether, by means of the crook, we can reach more faith, love, heavenly-mindedness, contempt of the world, humility, self-denial, and so on (2 Cor 6:10). So, while we lose on one side, we will gain on another.

4. Grace to sustain us under the crook (2 Cor 12:8, 9): “Three times I pleaded with the Lord.” Verse 9: “But He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you.’” Whether a man is faint and has a light burden, or is refreshed and strengthened and has a heavy one, it is all one: the second can go as easily under his burden as the first under his. Grace proportioned to the trial is what we should aim at. If we get that, then even though the crook is not made even, we are even with it.

Lastly, keeping in our eye the eternal rest and weight of glory in the other world (2 Cor 4:17, 18): “For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison, while we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen.” This will balance the crook in your lot, whatever it may be. Those who have no well-grounded hope of salvation will find the crook in their lot in this world such a weight that they have nothing to counterbalance it. But the hope of eternal rest may hold a man up under all the toil and labor he meets with here.

Exhortation 3. Let us then set ourselves to bear the crook in our lot rightly and to behave rightly under it, as long as God sees fit to continue it. What we cannot mend, let us bear as Christians, and not fight against God and so kick against the goads. Let us bear it in this way:

1. Patiently, without flaring up and fretting or murmuring (Jas 5:7; Ps 37:7). Though we lose our comfort in created things through the crook in our lot, let us not lose possession of ourselves (Luke 21:19). The crook in our lot makes us like a man who has only a scanty, chilly fire to warm himself at. But impatience under it scatters the fire, so as to set the house on fire around us, and that leaves us exposed (Prov 25:28): “Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not control his temper.”

2. With Christian fortitude, without sinking under discouragement: “do not lose heart when He rebukes you” (Heb 12:5). Satan’s work is to use the crook either to bend or to break people’s spirits, and often to break them by bending them. Our work is to behave evenly under it, steering a middle course, guarding against splitting on the rocks on either side. Our happiness does not lie in any earthly comfort, nor will the lack of any of them make us miserable (Hab 3:17, 18). So we are resolutely to hold on our way, with a holy contempt and disregard of the hardships (Job 17:9): “Yet a righteous one holds to his way, and the one with clean hands grows stronger.”

Quest. When is a man to be reckoned to have fallen under sinking discouragement from the crook in his lot? Answer. When it prevails so far as to unfit us for the duties either of our particular calling or of our Christian calling. We may be sure it has carried us beyond the bounds of moderate grief when it unfits us for the common affairs of life, which the Lord calls us to manage (1 Cor 7:24). It is recorded to Abraham’s credit (Gen 23:3, 4). Or when it unfits us for the duties of religion, either hindering them altogether (1 Pet 3:7), “so that your+ prayers will not be hindered,” cut off, or cut up, like a tree from the roots; or making a man quite hopeless in them (Mal 2:13).

Lastly, profitably, so that we may gain some advantage from it (Ps 119:71): “It was good for me to be afflicted, that I might learn Your statutes.” There is advantage to be made of it (Rom 5:3–5), and it is certainly a badly managed crook in our lot when we get no spiritual good from it (Heb 12:11). The crook is a kind of spiritual medicine. Medicine that purges away no infection is wasted, and its unpleasant taste and griping pains are endured in vain. In the same way, a crook that we are not made better by is a wasted crook, and its bitterness is badly spent (Isa 27:9): “By this, therefore, Jacob’s guilt will be purged, and this will be the full fruit of the removal of his sin.”

Motives to press this exhortation. Consider:

1. There will be no making it even while God sees fit to continue it. Let us behave under it as we will, and make what sallies we please against it, it will continue immovable, as if fixed with bands of iron and bronze (Job 23:13, 14): “But He is unchangeable, and who can oppose Him? He does what He desires.” Verse 14: “For He carries out what He has appointed for me, and He has many such plans.” Is it not wisdom, then, to make the best we can of what we cannot mend? Make a virtue, then, of necessity. What cannot be cured must be endured, and should be endured with Christian resignation.

2. Stubborn behavior under it greatly increases its pain. What makes the yoke chafe our necks, but that we struggle so much against it and cannot let it sit easily on us (Jer 31:18)? How often are we in that case like men dashing their heads against a rock to remove it! The rock stands unmoved, but they are wounded, and lose greatly by their struggle. Impatience under the crook lays an extra weight on the burden and makes it heavier, while at the same time it weakens us and makes us less able to bear it.

3. The crook in your lot is the special trial God has chosen for you, to take your measure by (1 Pet 1:6, 7). It is God’s fire, by which he tries what metal men are made of; heaven’s touchstone for revealing true and counterfeit Christians. Some whom the crook in the lot will show to be counterfeit may bear and go through several trials, because they can by no means bear that (Mark 10:21, 22). So think to yourself under it: “Now the trial of my state turns on this. By this I must be proved either sincere or a hypocrite.” For, (1.) can anyone be a subject of Christ from the heart without being able to submit his lot to him? Do not all who sincerely come to Christ put a blank sheet into his hand (Acts 9:6; Ps 47:4)? And does he not tell us that without that disposition we are not his disciples (Luke 14:26)? “If anyone comes to Me and does not hate his father and mother and wife and children and brothers and sisters—yes, even his own life—he cannot be My disciple.” Perhaps you find you can submit to anything but that. But will that but spoil everything (Mark 10:21)? Did anyone ever hear of a sincere embracing of Christ with a reservation or exception of one thing, in which they had to be their own lords?

Quest. Is that disposition, then, a qualification necessarily required before we believe? And if so, where must we get it? Can we work it out of our natural powers? Answer. No, it is not so. But it necessarily accompanies and goes along with believing, flowing from the same saving illumination in the knowledge of Christ by which the soul is brought to believe in him. By this the soul sees him to be an able Savior, and so trusts in him for salvation; and sees him to be the rightful Lord and infinitely wise Ruler, and so submits the lot to him (Matt 13:45, 46). The soul, taking him as Savior, takes him also as Head and Ruler. It is Christ’s giving himself to us, and our receiving him, that causes us to give up other things to him and for him, just as it is the light that dispels the darkness. Case. Alas! I cannot get my heart freely to submit my lot to him in that point. Answer. That submission will not be carried on in anyone without a struggle. The old man will never submit it, and when the new man of grace is submitting it, the old man will still be protesting (Gal 5:17): “For the flesh craves what is contrary to the Spirit, and the Spirit what is contrary to the flesh. They are opposed to each other, so that you+ cannot do what you+ want.” But are you+ sincerely desirous of submitting it, and habitually aiming at it? Do you+ turn away from the ungracious struggle against the crook to the struggle with your+ own heart, to bring it to submit, believing the promise and using the means for it, and being grieved from the heart with yourselves+ that you+ cannot submit? This is submitting your+ lot, in the favorable interpretation of the gospel (Rom 7:17–20; 2 Cor 8:12). If you+ had your+ choice, would you+ rather have your+ heart brought to submit to the crook than have the crook made even to your+ heart’s desire (Rom 7:22, 23)? And do you+ not sincerely endeavor to submit it in spite of the reluctance of the flesh (Gal 5:17)?

2. Where is Christian self-denial and the taking up of the cross, without submitting to the crook? This is the first lesson Christ puts into the hands of his disciples (Matt 16:24): “If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.” Self-denial would bring about a reconciliation with the crook and an acceptance of the cross. But while we cannot bear to have our corrupt self denied any of its cravings, and particularly that which God sees fit especially to deny it, we cannot bear the crook in our lot, but fight against it in favor of self.

3. Where is our conformity to Christ while we cannot submit to the crook? We cannot show ourselves to be Christians without conformity to Christ: “Whoever claims to abide in Him must walk as Jesus walked” (1 John 2:6). There was a continual crook in Christ’s lot, but he submitted to it (Phil 2:8): “And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross.” So also Rom 15:3: “For even Christ did not please Himself,” and so on. And so must we, if we would prove ourselves Christians indeed (Matt 11:29; 2 Tim 2:11, 12).

4. How will we prove ourselves the true-born children of God if we are still at war with the crook? We cannot pray, “Our Father … Your will be done, on earth as …” and so on (Matt 6). No, the language of that practice is, “We must have our own will, and God’s will does not satisfy us.”

Motive 4. The trial by the crook here will not last long (1 Cor 7:31). Though the work is hard, it may be borne all the better because it will not be long. A few days, or years at the most, will put an end to it and take you+ off your+ trials. Do not say, “I will never be eased of it.” For if you+ are not eased of it before, you+ will be eased of it at death, whatever may come in its place afterward. A serious view of death and eternity might move us to set ourselves to behave rightly under our crook while it lasts.

5. If you+ would set yourselves+ in a Christian manner to bear the crook, you+ would find it easier than you+ imagine (Matt 11:29, 30). “Take My yoke upon you+ and learn from Me … and you+ will find rest for your+ souls.” Verse 30: “For My yoke is easy and My burden is light.” Satan has no readier way to gain his purpose than to persuade men that it is impossible their minds should ever yield to the crook, and that it is an altogether unbearable burden to them. As long as you+ believe that, be sure you+ will never be able to bear it. But the Lord makes no crook in any man’s lot that the man cannot bear acceptably, though not sinlessly and perfectly (Matt 11:30). For strength for that purpose is secured in the covenant (2 Cor 3:5; Phil 4:13), and when it is fetched by faith, it will certainly come (Ps 28:7).

6. If you+ behave as Christians under your+ crook here, you+ will not lose your+ labor, but will get a full reward of grace in the other world, through Christ (2 Tim 2:12; 1 Cor 15:58). On this very ground a blessing is pronounced on the man who perseveres (Jas 1:12): “Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.” Heaven is the place into which those who are proved genuine upon the trial of the crook are received (Rev 7:14): “These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.” When you+ come there, no trace of the crook will remain in your+ lot, nor will you+ have the least uneasy memory of it; instead it will give emphasis to your+ praises and heighten your+ joy.

7. If you+ do not behave as Christians under it, you+ will lose your+ souls in the other world (Jude 15, 16). Those who are at war with God over their lot here, God will be at war with them forever. If they will not submit to his yoke here and go quietly under it, he will bind his yoke about their neck forever, with everlasting bonds that will never be loosed (Job 9:4).

Lastly, whatever crook is in anyone’s lot, it is very likely that a public crook awaits this generation that will be more trying. This is a day of sinning beyond the days of our fathers, a day in which God is making great crooks in the lot of those dearest to him. But these seem to foretell such a general, public crook awaiting the generation as will make our present private ones of very little weight (1 Pet 4:17, 18). Therefore set yourselves+ to behave rightly under the crook in your+ lot.

If you+ ask how one may reach that, we offer this for direction:

Doctrine Last.

Considering the crook in the lot as the work of God is a proper means to bring one to behave rightly under it.

I. What it is to consider the crook as the work of God, we set out in these five things.

1st. An inquiry into the spring from which it rises (Gen 25:22). Reason and religion both teach us not only to notice the crook, which we cannot avoid, but to consider and inquire into its spring. Surely it is not our choice, nor do we make it for ourselves on purpose. And to ascribe it to fortune is to ascribe it to nothing. It has not sprung up of itself, but is sown for us by one hand or another (Job 5:6). And we are to notice the hand it comes from.

2dly, a perceiving of the hand of God in it. Whatever hand any created thing has in it, we ought not to let our view stop at created things, but look above and beyond them to the agency of the supreme Manager in it (Job 1:21). Without this we make a god of a created thing that is the instrument of the crook, looking on it as if it were the first cause, which belongs to God alone (Rom 11:36). And we bring ourselves under that sentence (Ps 28:5): “Since they show no regard for the works of the Lord or what His hands have done, He will tear them down and never rebuild them.”

3dly, a representing of it to ourselves as the work of God, which he has brought about against us for holy and wise ends, befitting the divine perfections. This is to take it by the right handle, to represent it to ourselves under a right notion, from which right conduct under it may spring. It can never be safe to overlook God in it. But it is very safe to overlook the created instrument, ascribing the crook to God as if no other hand were in it, since his is always the principal hand in it: “He is the Lord. Let Him do what is good in His eyes” (1 Sam 3:18). So David overlooked Shimei, and looked to God in the matter of his cursing, as one would look past the axe and fix his eye on the man who wielded it. Here two things are to come into our consideration.

1. The decree of God, purposing that crook for us from eternity: “who works out everything by the counsel of His will” (Eph 1:11). This is the sealed book in which are written all the black lines that make the crook. Whatever valley of darkness, grief and sorrow we are carried through, we are to look on it as made by the mountains of bronze, the immovable divine purposes (Zech 6:1). This can be no presumption in that case, if we carry it no farther than the event goes in our sight and feeling; for so far the book is opened for us to look into.

2. The providence of God, bringing that crook to pass for us in time (Amos 3:6). Nothing can befall us without him in whom we live. Whatever kind of agency created things may have in the making of our crook, whatever they have done or not done toward it, he is the spring that sets all the created wheels in motion, and if he ceased, they would all stop. Yet he is always infinitely pure in his agency, however impure they are in theirs. Job considered both these things (Job 23:14).

4thly, a continuing in the thought of it as such. It is not a single glance of the eye, but a contemplating and leisurely viewing of it as his work, that is the proper means. We are to be:

(1.) Habitually impressed with this consideration. As the crook is some lasting grievance, so the consideration of this as the remedy should be habitually kept up. There are other considerations besides this one that we must entertain, so that we cannot always have it expressly in our minds. But we must lay it down as a rooted principle by which we are to manage the crook, and keep the heart in such a disposition that it may slip expressly into our minds as occasion requires.

(2.) Exercised in it as occasion arises. Whenever we begin to feel the smart of the crook, we should fetch in this remedy; when the yoke begins to chafe the neck, this spiritual ointment should be applied. And however often the smart comes in on us, it will be our wisdom to fetch in the consideration as the proper remedy. The more often it is used, the more easily it will come to hand, and also the more effectual it will be.

Lastly, a considering of it for the end for which it is set before us, namely, to bring us to dutiful behavior under it. Men’s corruption will lead them to enter on this consideration; and as the principle is, so will its end and effect be: corrupt (2 Kgs 6:33). But we must enter on it and use it for a good end, if we would have good of it, taking it as a practical consideration for regulating our conduct under the crook.

II. How it is to be understood to be a proper means to bring one to behave rightly under the crook.

1. Negatively, not as if it were sufficient of itself, standing alone, to produce that effect. But 2. Positively, as it is used in faith, in the faith of the gospel. That is to say, a sinner’s bare considering of the crook in his lot as the work of God, without any saving relation to God, will never be a way to behave rightly under it. But when he has believed in Jesus Christ, and so takes God for his God, the considering of the crook as the work of God, his own God, is the proper means to bring him to that desirable temper and behavior. Many hearers mistake here. When they hear such and such considerations from the law proposed for bringing them to duty, they at once imagine that they may gain the point by the mere force of them. And so do many preachers too, who forget Christ and the gospel and claim to make men Christians by the force of reason. The eyes of both are held, so that they do not see the corruption of men’s nature, which is such that it sets the true cure above the force of reason. All they are aware of is some bad habits, which they think may be shaken off by a vigorous use of their rational faculties. To clear this matter, consider:

First, is it reasonable to think of setting fallen man, with his corrupted nature, to work in the same way as innocent Adam? That is to set beggars on a level with the rich, and lame men on a journey with those who have the use of their limbs. Innocent Adam had a stock of gracious abilities, by which he might have brought himself, by the force of moral considerations, to perform duty rightly. But where is that stock with us (2 Cor 3:5)? Whatever force such considerations have on a soul endowed with spiritual life, what force do they have to raise the dead, such as we are (Eph 2:1)?

Secondly, the Scripture is very plain on this point, showing the indispensable necessity of faith (Heb 11), and of such faith as unites to Christ (John 15:5): “Without Me,” that is, separate from me, “you+ can do nothing”; no, not with all the moral considerations you+ can use. How were the Ten Commandments given on Mount Sinai? Not as bare demands of duty, but prefaced with the gospel, to be believed in the first place: “I am the Lord your God,” and so on. And so Solomon, whom many regard as a moral philosopher rather than an inspired writer leading to Christ, prefaces his writings, at the beginning of the Proverbs, with the most express gospel. And must we have it expressly repeated in our Bibles with every moral precept, or else shut our eyes and take these precepts without it? This is the effect of our natural enmity to Christ. If we loved him more, we would see him more on every page and in every command, receiving the law from his mouth.

Thirdly, only consider what it is to behave rightly under the crook in the lot: what humiliation of soul, self-denial, and absolute resignation to the will of God must be in it; from what love to God it must proceed; how regard for his glory must influence it as its chief end. Then try and see whether it is not impossible for you+ to reach it without the faith mentioned above. I know a Christian may reach it without full assurance. But still, according to the measure of their persuasion that God is their God, so will their attainments in it be; these keep equal pace. Oh, what kind of hearts do they imagine they have, who think they can empty them of created things for a moment any further than they can fill them with God, as their God, in its place! No doubt men may, by the force of moral considerations, work themselves into a behavior under the crook that is outwardly right, such as many pagans had. But a Christian disposition of spirit under it will never be reached without that faith in God.

Objection. Then it is only saints who are capable of making use of that consideration. Answer. Yes, indeed it is so, as with that and all other moral considerations, for truly Christian ends. And that amounts to no more than this: directions for walking rightly are only for the living, who have the use of their limbs. And therefore, so that we may make use of it, set yourselves+ to believe in the first place.

III. I will confirm that it is a proper means to bring one to behave rightly under the crook. This will appear if you+ consider these four things.

1. It is of great use to turn us away from considering and dwelling on those things about the crook which serve to irritate our corruption. Such are the frustrating of our wills and wishes; the satisfaction we would have in matters going according to our mind; the instruments of the crook, how injurious they are to us, how unreasonable, how obstinate, and so on. Dwelling on these considerations is only blowing the fire within. But to turn our eyes to the crook as the work of God would be a cure by way of diversion (2 Sam 6:9, 10). And such diversion of the thoughts is not only lawful, but profitable and necessary.

2. It has a moral fitness for producing the good effect. Though our cure is not brought about by the mere force of reason, yet it is carried on, not by a brute movement, but in a rational way (Eph 5:14). This consideration has a moral efficacy on our reason. It is fit to awe us into submission, and supplies much argument for it, moving us to behave as Christians under our crook.

3. It has a divine appointment for that end, which is to be believed (Prov 3:6; so also the text). A created thing in itself is inefficacious and motionless, a mere emptiness (Acts 17:28). To make anything a means fit for an end without believing this is to make a god of a created thing. Therefore it is to be used in dependence on God, according to his word of appointment (1 Tim 4:4, 5). And everything is fit for the end for which God has appointed it. This consideration is appointed for that end, and therefore it is a fit means for it.

Lastly, the Spirit may be expected to work by it, and does work by it in those who believe and look to him for it, since it is a means of his own appointment. Papists, Legalists and all superstitious persons devise various means of sanctification that seem to have, or really have, a moral fitness for it. But they are quite ineffectual, because, like Abana and Pharpar, they lack a word of divine appointment for curing us of our leprosy. Therefore the Spirit does not work by them, since they are none of his own tools, but devised out of their own hearts. And since the means of divine appointment are ineffectual without the Spirit, these can never be effectual. But this consideration has a divine appointment, so the Spirit works by it.

Use. Then take this direction for behaving rightly under the crook in your+ lot. Accustom yourselves+ to consider it as the work of God. And to help you+ make use of it so that it may be effectual, I offer this advice.

1. Consider it as the work of your+ God in Christ. This is the way to sprinkle it with gospel grace, and so to make it bearable (Ps 22:1, 2, 3). Discerning a Father’s hand in the crook will take away much of its bitterness and sugar the pill for you+. For this reason it will be necessary (1.) solemnly to take God for your+ God under your+ crook (Ps 142:4, 5); (2.) in all your+ encounters with it, resolutely to believe and claim your+ share in him (1 Sam 30:6).

2. Enlarge the consideration with a view of the divine relations to you+, and of the divine attributes. Consider that it is the work of your+ God, the work of your+ Father, elder Brother, Head, Husband, and so on, who therefore surely seeks your+ good. Consider his holiness and justice, which show that he does not wrong you+; his mercy and goodness, that it is not worse; his sovereignty, which may silence you+; his infinite wisdom and love, which may satisfy you+ in it.

3. Consider what a work of his it is: how it is a convicting work, for bringing sin to remembrance; a correcting work, to chastise you+ for your+ follies; a preventing work, to hedge you+ in from courses of sin you+ would otherwise be apt to run into; a trying work, to reveal your+ state, your+ graces and corruptions; a weaning work, to wean you+ from the world and fit you+ for heaven.

Lastly, in all your+ considerations of it in this way, look upward for the Spirit to make them effectual (1 Cor 3:6). So you+ may behave as Christians under it, until God makes it even, either here or in heaven.

Part II: A Humble Spirit with the Lowly

Prov 16:19.

Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud.

If men could once be brought to believe that it is better to have their minds brought to bend to the crook in their lot than to force even the crook itself to suit their mind, they would then be in a fair way to bring their affairs in that case to a good outcome. Here, then, is the divine decision in that case: “Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly than to divide the spoil with the proud.” In these words,

First, there is a comparison set up, and that between two parties, and two points in which they differ vastly.

1st. The parties are the lowly and the proud, who differ like heaven and the center of the earth. The proud are always climbing up and soaring aloft; the lowly are content to creep on the ground, if that is the will of God. Let us view them more particularly as the text represents them.

(1.) On the one hand is the lowly. Here there is a reading in the line of the text and one in the margin, both from the Holy Spirit, and they differ only in one letter. The former is the afflicted or poor, who are low in their condition: those who have a notable crook in their lot through affliction laid on them, by which their condition in the world is lowered. The other is the lowly, or the meek and humble ones, who are low in their spirit as well as in their condition, and so have their mind brought down to their lot. Both together make up the character of this lowly party.

(2.) On the other hand is the proud, the showy and haughty ones. It is supposed here that they too are crossed and have crooks in their lot; for dividing the spoil follows a victory, and a victory presupposes a battle.

2d. The points in which these parties are supposed to differ, namely, being of a humble spirit, and dividing the spoil.

Afflicted and lowly ones may sometimes have their condition changed. They may be raised up on high and divide the spoil, as Hannah, Job and others were. The proud may sometimes be thrown down and crushed, as Pharaoh, Nebuchadnezzar and others were. But that is not the question, whether it is better to be raised up with the lowly or thrown down with the proud. There would be no difficulty in deciding that. The question is this: is it better to be of a low and humble spirit, in low circumstances, with afflicted humble ones, or to divide the spoil and get one’s will with the proud? If men would speak the natural feelings of their hearts, that question would be decided against the text. The points compared here, and set one against the other, are these:

(1.) On the one hand, to be of a humble spirit with afflicted lowly ones. The Hebrew is to be of low spirit, for the word first of all denotes lowness in position or state. So the point proposed here is to be with afflicted lowly ones, or in their state, having the spirit brought down to that low lot, the lowness of the spirit balancing the lowness of one’s condition.

(2.) On the other hand, to divide the spoil with the proud. The point proposed here is to be with the proud, or in their state, having their lot brought by main force to their liking, like those who, believing themselves wronged, fight it out with the enemy, overcome, and divide the spoil as they please.

2. The decision made, in which the former is preferred to the latter: “Better …” If these two parties were set before us, it would be better to take our lot with those of a low condition who have their spirits brought as low as their lot, than with those who, being of a proud and high-bent spirit, have their lot brought up to their liking. A humbled spirit is better than a heightened condition.

Doctrine.

There is a generation of lowly afflicted ones, whose spirit is lowered and brought down to their lot, and whose case, in that respect, is better than that of the proud who get their will and carry everything to their liking.

I. We shall consider the generation of the lowly afflicted ones, whose spirit is brought down to their lot. And we shall, 1st, lay down some general considerations about them.

1. There is such a generation in the world, bad as the world is. The text expressly mentions them, and Scripture mentions them elsewhere, as in Ps 9:12 and 10:12, and Matt 5:3 with Luke 6:20. Where shall we look for them? Not in heaven: there are no afflicted ones there. Not in hell: there are no lowly or humble ones there, whose spirit is brought to their lot. So they must be in this world, where the state of trial is.

2. If it were not so, Christ, as he was in the world, would have no followers in it. He was the Head of that generation, whom they all copy: “Learn from Me, for I am gentle and lowly in heart” (Matt 11:29). And for his honor, and the honor of his cross, they will never be lacking as long as the world stands: “For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son” (Rom 8:29). His image lies in these two things, suffering and holiness, of which lowliness is a chief part.

3. Nevertheless they are certainly very rare in the world. Agur observes that there is another generation, quite opposite to them: “how haughty are their eyes and pretentious are their glances” (Prov 30:13). And this makes up by far the greatest company. The low and afflicted lot is not so very rare, but the lowly disposition of spirit is rarely yoked with it. Many a high-bent spirit stays bent high in spite of lowering circumstances.

4. They can be no more in number than the truly godly. For nothing less than the power of divine grace can bring men’s minds down from their natural height and make their will pliant to the will of God (2 Cor 10:4–5). Men may put on a face of submission to a low and crossed lot because they cannot help it and see that it is useless to strive. But to bring the spirit truly to it must be the work of humbling grace.

5. Though all the godly are of that generation, there are some of them to whom that character belongs more especially. The way to heaven lies through tribulation for all (Acts 14:22), and all Christ’s followers are reconciled to it nonetheless (Luke 14:26). Yet some of them are more remarkably disciplined than others, and their spirit is nevertheless humbled by it and brought down to their lot: “Surely I have stilled and quieted my soul; like a weaned child with his mother, like a weaned child is my soul within me” (Ps 131:2). “For I have learned to be content regardless of my circumstances. I know how to live humbly, and I know how to abound. I am accustomed to any and every situation—to being filled and being hungry, to having plenty and having need” (Phil 4:11–12).

Lastly, a lowly disposition of soul, and the habitual aim and bent of the heart that way, is very favorably interpreted in heaven. If we looked for a generation perfectly purged of pride, and of the heart’s risings against their adverse lot at any time, we would find none in this world. But those who sincerely aim and endeavor to reach it, and to keep the way of contented submission, returning to it again though they are sometimes blown aside, God counts to be that lowly generation (2 Cor 8:12; Jas 5:11).

II. We shall go into the particulars of their character. Three things together make up their character.

First, affliction in their lot. That lowly generation, preferred to the proud and prosperous, is a generation of afflicted ones, whom God keeps under the discipline of the covenant. We may sum it up in these two things.

1. A yoke of affliction of one kind or another is often upon them (Ps 73:14). If there is silence in heaven, it is only for half an hour (Rev 8:1). God is often visiting them, as a master visits his pupils and a physician his patients, whereas others are in a way overlooked by him (Rev 3:19). They are used to the yoke, and that from the time they enter God’s family (Ps 129:1–3). God sees that it is good for them (Lam 3:27–28).

2. There is a particular yoke of affliction which God has chosen for them. It hangs about them, and is seldom, if ever, off them (Luke 9:23). That is their special trial, the crook in their lot, the yoke which lies on them for their constant exercise. Their other trials may be changed, but that is a weight that hangs about them continually, bowing them down.

Secondly, lowliness in their disposition and the tenor of their spirit. They are a generation of lowly, humble ones, whose spirits God has by his grace brought down from their natural height. And so:

1. They think soberly and humbly of themselves: of what they are (2 Cor 12:11), what they can do (2 Cor 3:5), what they are worth (Gen 32:10), and what they deserve (Lam 3:22). Viewing themselves in the mirror of the divine law and perfection, they see themselves as a mass of imperfection and sinfulness (Job 42:5–6).

2. They think highly and honorably of God (Ps 144:3). They are taught by the Spirit what God is, and so they have exalted thoughts of him. They consider him as the Sovereign of the world, his perfections as infinite, his work as perfect. They look on him as the fountain of happiness, as a God in Christ who does all things well, and they trust his wisdom, goodness and love even where they cannot see (Heb 11:8).

3. They think favorably of others, as far as justice allows (Phil 2:3). Though they cannot keep themselves from seeing others’ glaring faults, they are ready at the same time to acknowledge their excellencies, and to esteem them for these as far as they go. And because they see more into their own mercies and advantages for holiness, and their own misuse of them, than they can see into those of others, they are inclined to look on others as better than themselves, when circumstances are compared.

4. They are sunk down into a state of subordination to God and his will (Ps 131:1–2). Pride sets a man up against God. Lowliness brings him back to his place and lays him down at the feet of his sovereign Lord, saying, “Your will be done, on earth …” They no longer seek the command, but are content that God himself should sit at the helm of their affairs and manage everything for them (Ps 47:4).

5. They are not bent on high things, but disposed to stoop to low things (Ps 131:1). Lowliness levels the towering imaginations which pride raises up against heaven. It draws a veil over all personal worth and excellencies before the Lord, and it yields a man’s all to the Lord, to serve as stepping stones to the throne of his glory (2 Sam 15:25–26).

Lastly, they are inclined to magnify the mercies given to them (Gen 32:10). Pride of heart overlooks and belittles the mercies one has, and fixes the eye on what is lacking in one’s condition. It makes one like the flies that pass over the sound places and swarm together on the sore. Lowliness, on the contrary, teaches men to count up the mercies they enjoy in the lowest condition, and to set a mark on the good things they have had, or still have (Job 2:10).

Thirdly, a spirit brought down to their lot. Their lot is a low and afflicted one, but their spirit is as low, being brought down to it through grace. We may sum it up in these five things:

1. They submit to it as just: “Because I have sinned against Him, I must endure the rage of the Lord” (Mic 7:9). There are no hardships in our condition that we have not brought on ourselves. So it is just that we kiss the rod and are silent under it, and so lower our spirits to our lot. If they complain, their complaints are against themselves. Their hearts do not rise up against the Lord; still less do they open their mouths against the heavens. They justify God and condemn themselves, revering his holiness and spotless righteousness in his proceedings against them.

2. They go quietly under it as bearable: “It is good to wait quietly for the salvation of the Lord. It is good for a man to bear the yoke while he is still young. Let him sit alone in silence, for God has disciplined him. Let him bury his face in the dust—perhaps there is still hope” (Lam 3:26–29). While the unsubdued spirit rages under the yoke like a bullock unaccustomed to it, the spirit brought to the lot goes softly under it. They see that it is of the Lord’s mercy that it is not worse. They take up the bare cross as God lays it down, without the extra weights that turbulent passions add to it. And so it really becomes easier than they thought it could have been, like a burden fitted to the back.

3. They are satisfied in it, drawing their comfort from another quarter than their outward condition, just as the house stands firm when a prop it did not lean on is taken away. “Though the fig tree does not bud and no fruit is on the vines, … yet I will exult in the Lord” (Hab 3:17–18). So David did in the day of his distress: he “found strength in the Lord his God” (1 Sam 30:6). It is a sign of a spirit not brought down to the lot when one is dejected and sunk under its hardships, as if one’s condition in the world were the point on which one’s happiness turned. It is the lack of mortification that makes men’s comforts wax and wane, ebb and flow, according to the various appearances of their lot in the world.

4. They take delight in it, as what is fit and good for them (Isa 39:8; 2 Cor 12:10). Men have a sort of satisfaction in the working of medicine, though it pains them sorely: they reason with themselves that it is good and best for them. So these lowly souls regard their afflicted lot as a spiritual medicine, necessary, fit and good for them, yes, best for them for the time, since it is administered by their heavenly Father. And so they reach a holy delight in their low afflicted lot.

The lowly spirit draws this sweetness out of the bitterness in the lot. It considers how the Lord, by means of that afflicting lot, stops the supply for unruly lusts, so that they may be starved; how he cuts off the side channels, so that the whole stream of the soul’s love may run toward himself; how he pulls off and holds off the man’s burden and hindrance of earthly comforts, so that he may run the more swiftly in the way to heaven.

Lastly, they rest in it, as what they do not wish to come out of until the God who brought them into it sees fit to bring them out with his good will (Isa 28:16). Though an unsubdued spirit’s time for deliverance is always ready, a humbled soul will be afraid of being taken out of its afflicted lot too soon. It will not push for a change until heaven moves to bring it about. Yet this does not hinder prayer and the use of appointed means, with dependence on the Lord, but requires faith, hope, patience and resignation (2 Sam 15:25–26).

II. We shall consider the generation of the proud who get their will and carry everything to their liking. In their character also there are three things.

First, crosses in their lot. They too have their trials allotted to them by overruling providence, and whatever circumstances in the world they may be in, they cannot escape them altogether. For consider:

1. The confusion and vanity brought into the creation by man’s sin have made it impossible to get through the world without meeting what will ruffle men (Eccl 1:14). Sin has turned the world from a paradise into a thicket; there is no getting through without being scratched. As the midges in summer will fly about those walking outdoors in fine clothes as well as about those in shabby clothes, so crosses in the world will meet the high as well as the low.

2. The pride of their heart exposes them particularly to crosses. A proud heart will make a cross for itself where a lowly soul would find none (Esth 5:13). It will make a real cross ten times heavier than it would be to the humble. The generation of the proud are like nettles and thorn-hedges, on which things flying about settle, while they pass over low and plain things. So none are more exposed to crosses than they are, though none are so unfit to bear them, as appears from what follows:

Secondly, reigning pride in their spirit. Their spirits were never subdued by a work of thorough humiliation; they remain at the height where the corruption of nature set them. That is why they can in no way bear the yoke God lays on them. The neck is swollen with the infection of pride and passion, so when the yoke once begins to touch it, they can have no more ease. We may view the case of the proud generation here in three things.

1. They value themselves too highly, and so the proud mind says the man should not stoop to the yoke; it is beneath him. What swelling vanity there is in this: “Who is the Lord that I should obey His voice?” (Exod 5:2). That is why a work of humiliation is necessary to make one take on the yoke, whether of Christ’s precepts or of his providence. The first error is in the understanding, which is why Solomon commonly calls a wicked man a fool. Accordingly the first stroke in conversion falls there too, humbling by conviction of sin. Men are bigger in their own conceit than they really are. So God, suiting things to what we really are, cannot please us.

2. They have an unmortified self-will, arising from that overvaluing of themselves, and it says he will not stoop (Exod 5:2). The question between Heaven and us is whether God’s will or our own must win the day. Our will is corrupt; God’s will is holy; they cannot agree. God says in his providence that our will must yield to his. But our will will not do that until the iron sinew in it is broken (Rom 8:7; Isa 48:4).

3. They have a crowd of unsubdued passions taking the side of self-will, and these say he shall not stoop (Rom 7:8–9). And so the war begins, and there is a field of battle within the man and outside him (Jas 4:1).

1st, a holy God crosses the self-will of proud creatures by his providence, overruling and disposing of things contrary to their inclination. Sometimes he does it by his own immediate hand, as in the case of Cain (Gen 4:4–5); sometimes by the hand of men who carry things against their wishes, as in the case of Ahab, to whom Naboth refused his vineyard (1 Kgs 21:4).

2dly, the proud heart and will, unable to submit to the cross or to bear being controlled, rises up against it and fights for the mastery with its whole force of unmortified passions. The aim is to remove the cross, that is, the crook, and to bring the thing to their own liking. This is the cause of this unholy war, in which:

(1.) One black band of hellish passions marches upward and attacks Heaven itself, namely discontent, impatience, murmuring, fretting and the like: “A man’s own folly subverts his way, yet his heart frets against the Lord” (Prov 19:3). These set the breast on fire and make the face fall (Gen 4:5). Sometimes they let off a volley of unseemly and passionate complaints (Jude 16), and sometimes of blasphemies (2 Kgs 6:33).

(2.) Another band marches forward and attacks the instrument or instruments of the cross, namely anger, wrath, fury, revenge, bitterness and the like (Prov 27:4). These carry the man out of the possession of himself (Luke 21:19). They fill the heart with a boiling heat (Ps 39:3) and the mouth with clamor and evil-speaking (Eph 4:31). Threats are breathed out (Acts 9:1), and sometimes they set the hands to work, with a most grievous outcome (Matt 10:21–22), as in the case of Ahab against Naboth.

So the proud carry on the war, but often they lose the day, and the cross remains immovable for all they can do. Yes, and sometimes they themselves fall in the quarrel, and it ends in their ruin (Exod 15:9–10). But that is not the case in the text. We are to consider them as:

Thirdly, getting their will and carrying everything to their liking. This speaks of:

1. Holy providence yielding to the man’s unmortified self-will, and letting things go as he wishes (Gen 6:3). God sees fit to let his striving with him drop, for it does not prevail for his good (Isa 1:5). So the reins are laid on the proud man’s neck, and he has what he was after: “Ephraim is joined to idols; leave him alone!” (Hos 4:17).

2. The lust remaining in its strength and vigor: “They were not turned from their lust” (Ps 78:30). God, in the way of his covenant, sometimes gives his people their will and sets them where they would be. But then, in that case, the lust for the thing is mortified, and they are like weaned children (Ps 10:17). But here the lust remains rampant; the proud seek food for it, and get it.

3. The cross removed and the yoke taken off (Ps 78:29). They could not think of bringing their mind to their lot, but opposed it, wrestled and fought against it, until it was brought up to their liking. So the day is theirs; the victory is on their side.

4. Lastly, the man is pleased at having carried his point, just as one is when he is dividing the spoil (1 Kgs 21:18–19).

Thus the case of the afflicted lowly generation, and of the proud generation prospering, is stated. Now,

III. I am to confirm the doctrine, or the decision of the text: that the case of the former is better than that of the latter. It is better to be in a low afflicted condition, with the spirit humbled and brought down to the lot, than to be of a proud and high spirit, having the lot brought up to it and matters going according to one’s will and wish, as one likes. This will appear from the following considerations:

First, humility is so far preferable to pride that in no circumstances whatever can it fail to be preferable. Let all the afflictions in the world attend the humble spirit, and all the prosperity in the world attend pride, humility will still have the better of it, as gold in a dunghill is more excellent than the same amount of lead in a cabinet. For:

1. Humility is a part of the image of God. Pride is the masterpiece of the image of the devil. Let us look at him who was the express image of the Father’s person, and we shall see him meek and lowly in heart (Matt 11:29). None was more afflicted, yet his spirit was perfectly brought down to his lot: “He was oppressed and afflicted, yet He did not open His mouth” (Isa 53:7). That is a shining part of the divine image. For though God cannot be low in his state and condition, yet he stoops in infinite grace (Isa 57:15). None forbears as he does (Rom 2:4), nor patiently suffers so much opposition to his will. This is set before us for our encouragement in affliction, as it shone in Christ: “Consider Him who endured such hostility from sinners, so that you+ will not grow weary and lose heart” (Heb 12:3).

Pride, on the other hand, is the very image of the devil (1 Tim 3:6). Will we pride ourselves on the height of our spirits? Satan will compete with the highest of us on that point. For though he is the most miserable, he is the proudest in the whole creation. There is the greatest distance between his spirit and his lot: the one is as high as the throne of God, the other as low as hell. And as it is impossible that his lot should ever be brought up to his spirit, so his spirit will never come down to his lot. Therefore he will be eternally at war with his lot. That is why, even now, he has no rest, but goes about seeking rest, and finds none.

Now, is it not better to be like God than like the devil? Like him who is the fountain of all good, rather than him who is the spring and sink of all evil? Can anything possibly tip the balance here and turn the preference to the other side? Then “better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly …”

2. Humility and lowliness of spirit fit us for friendly communion and fellowship with God in Christ. Pride makes God our enemy (1 Pet 5:5). Our happiness here and hereafter depends on our friendly fellowship with heaven. If we do not have that, nothing can make up our loss (Ps 30:5). If we have it, nothing can make us miserable: “If God is for us, who can be against us?” (Rom 8:31). Now, who are those whom God is for, but the humble and lowly? They are those who, being in Christ, are made like him in this. He blesses them and declares them heirs to the crown of glory: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt 5:3). He will look to them, however low their condition may be, while he overlooks others (Isa 66:2). He will have regard for them, however they may be despised: “Though the Lord is on high, He attends to the lowly; but the proud He knows from afar” (Ps 138:6). He will dwell with them, however poorly they dwell (Isa 57:15). He will certainly exalt them in due time, however low they lie now (Isa 40:4).

Whom is he against? Whom does he resist? The proud. Them he curses (Jer 17:5), and that curse will at length dry up their arm. The proud man is God’s rival. He makes himself his own god, and would have those around him make him theirs too. He rages and blusters if they will not fall down before him. But God will bring him down (Isa 40:4; Ps 18:27).

Now, is it not better to be fit for communion with God than to have him set against us on any terms?

3. Humility is a duty pleasing to God; pride is a sin pleasing to the devil (Isa 57:15; 1 Tim 3:6). God requires us to be humble, especially under affliction: “… clothe yourselves with humility” (1 Pet 5:5–6). That is our fitting garment. The humble tax collector was accepted, the proud Pharisee rejected. We may say of the generation of the proud, as in 1 Thess 2:16, “the utmost wrath has come upon them.” They please neither God nor men, but only themselves and Satan, whom they resemble in this. Now, duty is always better than sin, on any terms.

Secondly, those whose spirits are brought down to their afflicted lot have much quiet and rest of mind, while the proud, who must have their lot brought up to their liking, have much unrest, trouble and vexation. Consider here, on the one hand:

1. Quiet of mind and ease within is a great blessing, on which the comfort of life depends. Without it, nothing can make one’s life happy (Dan 5:6). And where it is kept, nothing can make life miserable (John 16:33). When this is secured in God, defiance is given to all the troubles of the world (Ps 46:2–4), like the child sailing in the midst of the rolling waves.

2. The spirit brought down to the lot creates and keeps this inward calm. All our trouble in our lot in the world rises from our mind’s disagreement with it. Let the mind be brought to the lot, and the whole tumult is instantly hushed. Let it be kept in that disposition, and the man will stand at ease in his affliction, like a rock unmoved by the waters beating on it: “Let the peace of Christ rule in your+ hearts, for to this you+ were called” (Col 3:15).

On the other hand, consider:

1. What disquiet of mind the proud suffer before they can get their lot brought up to their liking. “They have taught their tongues to lie; they wear themselves out committing iniquity” (Jer 9:5). “You+ crave what you+ do not have; you+ kill and covet, but are unable to obtain it. You+ quarrel and fight. You+ do not have …” (Jas 4:2). What arrows of grief go through their heart? What torture of anxiety, fretting and vexation must they endure? What contrary passions fight within them, and what outbursts of passion do they make? What unease Haman was in before he could carry his point of revenge against Mordecai by obtaining the king’s decree!

2. When the thing is got as they wished, it will not be worth the cost. Having it does not bring as much satisfaction and pleasure as the lack of it gives pain. This was evident in Rachel’s case as to having children, and in the case of Ps 78:30–31. There is a dead fly in the ointment that spoils the fragrance they expected to find in it. Fruit plucked from the tree of providence before it is ripe will readily set the teeth on edge. It proves like the manna kept overnight (Exod 16:20).

3. They have no sure hold on it; it does not last with them. Either it is soon taken from them, and they are just where they were before: “In My anger I gave you a king, and in My wrath I took him away” (Hos 13:11). Having a root of pride, it quickly withers away. Or else they are taken from it, so that they have no opportunity to enjoy it. So Haman obtained the decree, but before the day of its execution came he was gone.

Thirdly, those who get their spirit brought down to their afflicted lot gain a point far more valuable than those who in their pride force their lot up to their liking: “He who is slow to anger is better than a warrior, and he who rules his spirit is greater than one who captures a city” (Prov 16:32). This will appear if we consider:

1. The latter makes only a better condition in outward things; the former makes a better man. Life is more than food. The man himself is more valuable than all the outward conveniences that attend him. So what betters the man is preferable to what betters only his condition. Suppose two are sick. One has himself carried from a coarse bed to a fine one, but his sickness remains. The other lies still in the coarse bed, but his sickness is removed. Who doubts that the case of the latter is preferable? So it is here.

2. The subduing of our passions is more excellent than having the whole world subdued to our will. For then we are masters of ourselves, as Luke 21:19 has it, whereas in the other case we are still slaves to the worst of masters (Rom 6:16). In the one case we are safe, whatever storm may blow; in the other we lie exposed to thousands of dangers: “Like a city whose walls are broken down is a man who does not rule his spirit” (Prov 25:28).

Lastly, when both come to be judged, it will appear that the one has multiplied the tally of his good works by bringing his spirit to his lot, and the other the tally of his evil works by bringing his lot to his spirit. We have to do with an all-knowing God, in whose eyes every inward action is a work, good or bad, to be accounted for (Rom 2:16).

An afflicted lot is painful, but where it is well managed it is very fruitful. It exercises the graces of the Spirit in a Christian, which would otherwise lie dormant. But there is never an act of resignation to the will of God under the cross, nor an act of trusting in him for his help, that will not be recorded in Heaven’s register as a good work (Mal 3:16). And these are occasioned by affliction.

On the other hand, there is never a rising of the proud heart against the lot, nor a faithless attempt to bring the lot to our liking, whether it succeeds or not, that does not pass for an evil work before God. How greatly, then, will the tally of such works be multiplied by the war in which this spoil is divided!

USE I. Of information. From this we may learn:

1. It is not always best for people to get their will. There are many who cannot be pleased with God’s will for them, and they get their own will with a vengeance: “Israel would not obey Me. So I gave them up to their stubborn hearts to follow their own devices” (Ps 81:11–12). It may be the most pleasant and welcome for the time, but it is not the safest. So let people not pride themselves on carrying things that way by a strong hand; let them not triumph in such a victory. The reckoning afterward will open their eyes.

2. The afflicted, crossed party, whose lot is kept low, is so far from being a loser by it that he is a gainer, if his spirit is brought down to it. And if he will look at his case in the light of God’s unerring word, he is better off than if he had got everything carried his way. In the one way the vessels of wrath are fitted for destruction (Ps 78:29–31). In the other the vessels of mercy are fitted for glory, and so God disciplines his own (Lam 3:27).

3. It is better to yield to providence than to fight it out, even if we should win. Yielding to the sovereign disposal is both our fitting duty and our greatest advantage. Taking that way, we act most honorably: for what honor can there be in a creature disputing his ground with his Creator? And we act most wisely: for whatever the outcome of some battles in that case, we may be sure the victory in the war will be on Heaven’s side: “for by his own strength shall no man prevail” (1 Sam 2:9).

Lastly, it is of far greater concern for us to get our spirits brought down than to get our outward condition raised. But who believes this? All men strive to raise their outward condition; most men never give a thought to bringing down their spirits, and few apply themselves to it. And what is that but to be concerned to give drink to the thirsty sick, but never to think of seeking a cure for them that would carry off their thirst?

USE II. As you+ meet with crosses in your+ lot in the world, let your+ bent be rather to get your+ spirit humbled and brought down than to get the cross removed. I do not mean that you+ should not use all lawful means for the removal of your+ cross, in dependence on God, but only that you+ should be more concerned to get your+ spirit to bow and bend than to get the crook in your+ lot made even.

Motive 1. It is far more needful for us to have our spirits humbled under the cross than to have the cross removed. The removal of the cross is needful only for the ease of the flesh; the humbling is needful for the profit of our souls, to purify them and bring them into a state of health and cure.

2. The humbling of the spirit will have a very good effect on a crossed lot, but the removal of the cross will have none on the unhumbled spirit. The humbling will lighten the cross greatly for the time (Matt 11:30), and in due time carry it clean off (1 Pet 5:6). But the removal of the cross is no means of humbling the unhumbled. Though it may prevent irritation, the disease still remains.

Lastly, think with yourselves+ how dangerous and hopeless a case it is to have the cross removed before the spirit is humbled. That is to have the means of cure pulled away and blocked up from us while the power of the disease is still unbroken. It is to be taken off trials before we have given any good proof of ourselves, and so to be given up by our physician as hopeless (Isa 1:5; Hos 4:17).

For direction: believing the gospel, take God for your+ God in Christ toward your+ eternal salvation. Then dwell much on thoughts of God’s greatness and holiness, and of your+ own sinfulness. So you+ will be humbled under the mighty hand of God, and in due time he will lift you+ up.

Part III: Under the Mighty Hand of God

1 Pet 5:6.

Humble yourselves+, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that in due time He may exalt you+.

In the earlier part of this chapter the apostle presses the duties of church officers toward the people, and then the duty of the people, both toward their officers and among themselves, which he sums up in one word, submission. For this reason he recommends humility as the great means to bring all to their respective duties. This is enforced with an argument taken from the different treatment the Lord gives to the proud and to the humble: he opposes the one and shows favor to the other. Our text is an exhortation drawn from that consideration, and in it we have:

1. The duty we are therefore to make our aim: “Humble yourselves+, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that in due time He may exalt you+.” And here we may notice:

(1.) The state of those to whom it is proposed: those under the mighty hand of God, whom his hand has humbled, or placed low in some way in their circumstances in the world. And by these, I think, are meant not only those who are under particular, notable afflictions, which is the lot of some, but also those who by the providence of God are lowered in any way at all, which is the lot of all. All are in a state of submission or dependence on others. God has made this life a state of trial, and for that reason he has, by his mighty hand, made men subject one to another: wives, children and servants to husbands, parents and masters, and these again to their superiors. Among them, again, even the highest depend on those under them, as magistrates and ministers depend on the people, even the supreme magistrate being major singulis, minor universis [greater than each one, less than all together]. God has made this state of the world for the trial of men in their several stations and in their dependence on others. And therefore, when the time of trial is over, this state also comes to an end: “Then the end will come, … after He has destroyed all dominion, authority, and power” (1 Cor 15:24–25). Meanwhile, while it lasts, it makes humility necessary for all, to prompt them to the duty they owe their superiors, to whom God’s mighty hand has subjected them.

(2.) The duty itself, namely the humiliation of our spirits under the humbling circumstances the Lord has placed us in: “Humble yourselves+, therefore, under the mighty hand of God, that in due time He may exalt you+.” We may be under particular afflictions, which have cast us down from the height we were once at; or we may only be inferiors in one or more relationships; or, as is most common, both may be our case. Whichever it is, we must in this look to the mighty hand of God, as that which placed us there and is over us there to hold us down in it. And so, with a reverent awe of it, we must crouch down under it in the temper and disposition of our spirit, suiting our spirits to our lot, and careful to perform the duty of our low sphere.

(3.) A particular spring of this duty, therefore, which we must consider, is this. Those who cannot quietly keep the place God has assigned them in their afflictions or relationships, but keep pressing upward against the mighty hand that is over them, are resisted by that mighty hand, which throws them down, and often farther down than before. But it treats with grace and favor those who settle themselves under it to a quiet discharge of their duty in their situation. So, keeping our eye on this, we must set ourselves to humble ourselves.

2. The unfailing outcome of that course: “that in due time He may exalt you+.” The particle that is not always to be understood of purpose, as denoting the end or design the agent sets before himself, but sometimes only of outcome, as denoting the event or result of the action (John 9:2; 1 John 2:19). So here the meaning is not “humble yourselves+” with the design that “He may exalt you+,” but that it will end in his exalting you+. Compare Jas 4:10.

(1.) Here a happy outcome of humiliation of spirit is secured, namely exaltation, or lifting up on high by the power of God: “that … He may exalt you+.” Exaltation will as surely follow humiliation of spirit suited to the low condition as the morning follows the night, or the sun rises after the dawn. And these words are fitted to meet in advance the objections that the world and our corrupt hearts are apt to make against bringing the spirit down to the low condition.

Object. 1. If we let our spirit fall, we will always lie among people’s feet, and they will trample on us. Answer. No. Pride of spirit unsubdued will bring men to lie among the feet of others forever (Isa 66:24). But humiliation of spirit will without doubt bring them out from among their feet (Mal 4:2–3). Those who humble themselves now will be exalted forever; they will be brought out of their low situation and circumstances. Cast yourselves+ right down, then, with your+ low lot, and be assured you+ will not lie there.

Object. 2. If we do not raise ourselves, no one will raise us, and therefore we must see to it ourselves to do ourselves justice. Answer. That is wrong. Humble yourselves+ in your+ spirits, and God will raise you+ up in your+ lot or low condition. And those who have God pledged to raise them have no reason to say they have no one to do it for them. Bringing down the spirit is our duty; raising us up is God’s work. Let us not forfeit the privilege of God’s raising us up by claiming that work for ourselves and taking it out of his hand.

Object. 3. But surely we will never rise high if we let our spirits fall. Answer. That is wrong too. God will not only raise the humble ones, but will lift them up on high, for that is what the word means. At length they will be as high as ever they were low, however low that was. Indeed, the exaltation will be in proportion to the humiliation.

(2.) Here is the date of that happy outcome, when it will come about: in due time, or in the season, the proper season for it: “in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up” (Gal 6:9). We are apt to grow weary in humbling, trying circumstances, and we would always have our heads up (John 7:6). But Solomon observes that there is a time for everything when it does best, and the wise will wait for it (Eccl 3). There is a time too for exalting those who humble themselves. God has set it, and it is the due time for the purpose, the time when it does best, just as sowing is in the spring and reaping in the harvest. When that time comes, your+ exalting will no longer be put off, and it would come too soon if it came before that time.

Doctrine I.

The bent of one’s heart, in humbling circumstances, should lie toward a suitable humbling of the spirit, as under God’s mighty hand placing us in them.

I. Some things supposed in this. It supposes and implies that:

1. God brings men into humbling circumstances (Ezek 17:24): “Then all the trees of the field will know that I am the Lord. I bring the tall tree down.” There is a root of pride in the hearts of all men on earth, and it must be mortified before they can be fit for heaven. Therefore no man can fail to meet, in this time of trial, with some things that will put him to the proof whether he can stoop or not. And God brings men into humbling circumstances for that very end (Deut 8:2): “These forty years the Lord your God led you all the way in the wilderness, so that He might humble you and test you in order to know what was in your heart.”

2. These circumstances press like a weight on the heart, tending to bear it down (Ps 107:12): “He humbled their hearts with hard labor.” They go against the grain of the heart and cross its natural inclination. From this a trial naturally arises: whether the man can yield under God’s mighty hand or not, when God lays it on him; and so, whether he is fit for heaven or not.

3. The heart is naturally apt to rise against these humbling circumstances, and so against the mighty hand that brings them on and keeps them on. The man naturally bends his strength to get the weight off, so that he may lift up his head. He seeks more to please himself than to please his God (Job 35:9–10): “Men cry out under great oppression; they plead for relief from the arm of the mighty. But no one asks, ‘Where is God my Maker?’” This is the first way the heart runs in humbling circumstances, and the unsubdued spirits keep on in this way.

4. But what God requires is that we labor to bring down the heart rather than to get up the head (Jas 4:10). Here lies the proof of one’s fitness for heaven. One is on the way heavenward when he is more concerned to get his heart down than his head up, to go calmly under his burden than to get it off, to crouch under the mighty hand than to push it off him.

Lastly, In humbling circumstances there must be a noticing of God as the party we are dealing with: “Heed the rod and the One who ordained it” (Mic 6:9). There is an abjectness of spirit by which some give themselves up to the will of others under the harshest treatment, merely to please them, without regard to the authority and command of God. This is real baseness of spirit, by which one lies quietly to be trampled on by a fellow worm, out of regard for the weight he imagines that worm to have. And none fall into it so readily as the proud, at times, to serve their own turn (Acts 12:22). These are men-pleasers (Eph 6:6 with Galatians 1:10).

II. What are these humbling circumstances into which the mighty hand brings men? Taking for granted here what was taught before, that the crook in the lot is of God’s making, these are circumstances:

1. Of imperfection. God has placed all men in such circumstances, under a variety of deficiencies and imperfections (Phil 3:12). We can look nowhere without being beset by them. There is a heap of natural and moral imperfections about us: our bodies, and our souls in all their faculties, are in a state of imperfection. The pride of all glory is stained. It is a shame to us not to be humbled under such deficiencies as attend us; it is like a beggar strutting in his rags.

2. Of inferiority in relationships. In these, men are set in the lower place in relationships and society, and made to depend on others (1 Cor 7:24). To try men’s submission to himself, God has subjected them to others whom he has set over them, to show what regard they will pay to his authority and commands at second hand. Dominion or superiority is a part of the divine image (1 Cor 11:7). And therefore reverence toward superiors is necessarily required, consisting in an awed regard for that ray of the divine image shining in them (Eph 5:33; Heb 12:9, compare Ps 111:9). The same holds in all other relationships and superiorities, namely, that superiors stand so far in the place of God to those under them (Ps 82:6). And though the persons are worthless in themselves, that does not release one from the debt owed to them (Acts 23:4–5; Rom 13:7). The reason is that it is not their qualities but their station which is the ground of that debt of reverence and subjection. And the trial God takes of us in that matter turns not on the former but on the latter.

Now, since God has placed us in these circumstances of inferiority, all stubborn resistance, in anything not contrary to the command of God, is a rising up against his mighty hand (Rom 13:2). For God’s hand is on us for that purpose through others, though it is man’s hand that is directly on us.
