3. Of contradiction, which tends directly to thwart our will. This was a part of our Lord’s state of humiliation, and the apostle supposes it will be a part of ours too (Heb 12:3). There is perfect harmony in heaven; no one contradicts another there, for they are in their state of reward and exaltation. But we are here in our state of trial and humiliation, and therefore we cannot escape contradiction, however high we are placed.

Whether these contradictions are just or unjust, God brings men to meet them in order to humble them, to break them off from clinging to their own will, and to teach them resignation and self-denial. They are humbling in their own nature, and are much the same to us as the breaking of a horse or a bullock is to them. And I believe there are many cases in which they can be accounted for in no other way than by going back to this use God has for them.

4. Of affliction (Prov 16:19). Prosperity puffs up sinners with pride; and oh, how hard it is to keep a low spirit with a high and prosperous lot! But by affliction God calls men down from their heights to sit in the dust. He plucks away the jay-feathers in which they prided themselves, and rubs the paint and varnish off the creature, so that it appears in its native deformity. There are various kinds of affliction, some more humbling and some less, but all of them are humbling.

So then, not to lower the spirit under affliction is to attempt to rise up while God is forcefully casting us down and holding us down. If it is continued in, it cannot fail to provoke the Lord to break us in pieces (Ezek 24:13). For the afflicting hand is mighty.

Lastly, Of sin as the punishment of sin. We may allude here to Job 30:19. All the sin in the world is a punishment of Adam’s first sin. Man threw himself into the mire at first, and now he is justly left wallowing in it. Men willfully take one false step, and for that reason they are justly left to take another, worse one; and sin clings to all, even the best. And God overrules this for our humiliation, so that we may be ashamed and never open our mouth any more. So then, not to be humble under our sinfulness is to rise up against the mighty hand of God. It is to justify all our sinful departures from him, as men lost to all sense of duty and void of shame.

III. What it is, in humbling circumstances, to humble ourselves under the mighty hand of God. This is the great thing to be aimed at in our humbling circumstances, and we may sum it up in these eight things.

1. Noticing the mighty hand as at work in bringing about everything that concerns us, whether by way of efficacy or of permission (1 Sam 3:18): “And he said, ‘It is the Lord. Let Him do what is good in His eyes.’” And 2 Sam 16:10: “But the king replied, ‘If he curses me because the Lord told him, “Curse David,” who can ask, “Why did you do this?”’” God is the Fountain of all perfection, but we must trace our imperfections to his sovereign will. It is he who by his providence has posted everyone in his station. Without him we could not meet with such contradictions, for “the king’s heart is a waterway in the hand of the Lord He directs it where He pleases” (Prov 21:1). He sends afflictions, and he justly punishes one sin with another (Isa 6:10).

2. A sense of our own worthlessness and nothingness before him (Ps 144:3). Looking to the infinite majesty of the mighty hand that deals with us, we should say with Abraham, “I am but dust and ashes” (Gen 18:27), and say amen to the cry, “All flesh is like grass,” etc. (Isa 40:6). Keeping up thoughts of our own excellence under the pressure of the mighty hand is the very thing that swells the heart with pride and makes it rise up against that hand. And letting all such thoughts of ourselves fall before the eyes of his glory is the humbling that is required.

3. A sense of our guilt and filthiness (Rom 3:10; Isa 64:6). The mighty hand presses us down only as sinners. It is fitting, then, that under it we should see our sinfulness: our guilt, by which we will appear as criminals justly made to suffer; and our filthiness, by which we may be brought to loathe ourselves. And then we will think that nothing lays us lower than we well deserve. It is overlooking our sinfulness that allows the proud heart to swell.

4. A silent submission under the hand of God. His sovereignty claims this from us (Rom 9:20): “But who are you, O man, to talk back to God?” Nothing but unsubdued loftiness and pride of spirit can allow us to answer back under the sovereign hand. A view of the sovereign hand humbled the psalmist and awed him into submission with a profound silence (Ps 39:9): “I have become mute; I do not open my mouth because of what You have done.” So Job 1:21: “The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away. Blessed be the name of the Lord.” And Job 40:4–5: “How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth. I have spoken once, but I have no answer—twice, but I have nothing to add.” So Eli (1 Sam 3:18): “It is the Lord. Let Him do what is good in His eyes.”

5. A magnifying of his mercies toward us in the midst of all his proceedings against us (Ps 144:3). Has he laid us low? If we are duly humbled, we will wonder that he has not laid us lower (Ezra 9:13). For however low the humble are laid, they will see that they are not yet as low as their sins deserve (Lam 3:22).

6. A holy and silent wonder at the ways and counsels of God, as unsearchable to us (Rom 11:33). Pride of heart thinks nothing is too high for the man. So it arraigns the divine proceedings before its own tribunal, claims to see through them, censures them freely, and condemns them. But humiliation of spirit disposes a man to think with awe and honor of the mysteries of providence that he is not able to see through.

7. A forgetting and laying aside, before the Lord, of all our dignity by which we excel others (Rev 4:10). Pride feeds itself on the man’s real or imagined personal excellence and dignity. Being so used to it before others, it cannot forget it before God (Luke 18:11): “God, I thank You that I am not like the other men.” But humiliation of spirit makes it all vanish before him, as the shadow does before the shining sun, and it lays the man lower in his own eyes than anyone. “Surely I am the most brutish of men, and I lack the understanding of a man” (Prov 30:2).

Lastly, A ready submission to the lowliest services that are required by, or fitting to, our circumstances. At every turn pride finds something that is beneath the man to condescend or stoop to, measuring by his own mind and will, not by the circumstances God has placed him in. But humility measures by the circumstances one is placed in, and readily falls in with what they require. Our Savior gives us an example of this (Phil 2:8: “He humbled Himself and became obedient to death”), to be imitated (John 13:14): “So if I, your+ Lord and Teacher, have washed your+ feet, you+ also should wash one another’s feet.”

USE. Let the bent of your+ heart, then, in all your+ humbling circumstances, be toward the humbling of your+ spirit, as under the mighty hand of God. This lies in two things.

1. Carefully notice all your+ humbling circumstances, and overlook none of them. Observe your+ imperfections, your+ inferiority in relationships, the contradictions you+ meet with, your+ afflictions, the uncertainty of all things around you+, and your+ sinfulness. Look through them deliberately, and consider the steps of providence’s guidance of you+ in these, so that you+ may know yourselves+, and may not be strangers at home, blind to your+ own real state and condition.

2. Observing what these circumstances require of you+ as suited to them, bend your+ efforts toward it: to bring your+ spirits into that temper of humiliation, so that, as your+ lot is really low in all these respects, your+ spirits may be low too, as under the mighty hand of God. Let this be your+ great aim through your+ whole life, and your+ exercise every day.

Motive 1. God is certainly at work to humble every one of us. However high any are lifted up in this world, providence has hung certain badges of humiliation on them, whether they will notice them or not (Isa 40:6). Now it is our duty to fall in with the design of providence, so that while God is humbling us we may be humbling ourselves, and may not receive humbling dispensations in vain.

2. The humiliation of our spirits will not take effect without our own agency in it. While God is working on us in that way, we must work together with him, for he works on us as rational agents, who, being moved, move themselves (Phil 2:12–13). God by his providence may force down our lot and condition without us, but the spirit must come down voluntarily and by choice, or not at all. Therefore join in with humbling providences by humbling yourselves+, as sailors spread the sails when the wind begins to blow, so that they may run before it.

3. If you+ do not, you+ resist the mighty hand of God (Acts 7:51). You+ resist insofar as you+ do not yield, but stand like a rock, keeping your+ ground against your+ Maker in humbling providence (Jer 5:3): “You struck them, but they felt no pain. You finished them off, but they refused to accept discipline. They have made their faces harder than a rock and refused to repent.” Much more do you+ resist when you+ work against him to force up your+ condition, which you+ may see God means to hold down. And of this resistance consider:

(1.) Its sinfulness, what an evil thing it is. It is a direct fighting against God, a shaking off of subjection to our sovereign Lord, and a rising in rebellion against him (Isa 45:9).

(2.) Its folly. How unequal is the match! How can the struggle end well? (Job 9:4). What else can possibly be the outcome when the potsherds of the earth dash against the Rock of Ages, but that they are broken to pieces? We must say as in Job 41:8. All men must certainly bow or break under the mighty hand.

4. This is the time of humiliation, namely the time of this life. Everything is “beautiful in its time,” and the bringing down of the spirit now is beautiful, as in its proper time, just as the plowing and sowing of the ground is in the spring. Consider:

(1.) Humiliation of spirit is “precious in God’s sight” (1 Pet 3:4). As he has a special aversion to pride of heart, he has a special liking for humility (ch. 5:5). The humbling of sinners, and the bringing of them down from the heights where the corruption of their nature has set them, is the great end of his word and of his providences.

(2.) It is no easy thing to humble men’s spirits. It is not a little that will do it; it is a work that is not soon done. There is need of digging deep for a thorough humiliation in the work of conversion (Luke 6:48). Many a stroke must be given at the root of the tree of the heart’s natural pride before it falls. Often it seems to be fallen, and yet it rises again. And even when the root-stroke has been given in believers, the rod of pride buds again, so that there is still occasion for new humbling work.

(3.) The whole time of this life is appointed for humiliation. This was signified by the forty years the Israelites had in the wilderness (Deut 8:2). It was so for Christ, and therefore it must be so for men (Heb 12:2). And in that time they must either be formed according to Christ’s image, or else appear as reprobate silver that will by no means take it on (Rom 8:29). So whatever lifting up men may now and then get in this life, its habitual course will still be humbling.

(4.) There is no humbling afterward (Rev 22:11). If the pride of the heart is not brought down in this life, it never will be; no genuine humiliation is to be expected in another life. There the proud will be broken in pieces, but not softened. Their lot and condition will be brought to the lowest point, but the unhumbleness of their spirits will still remain. For this reason they will be in eternal agonies, through the opposition between their spirits and their lot (Rev 16:21).

So beware lest you+ let your+ time of humiliation slip by. Humbled we must be, or we are gone forever; and this is the time, the only time, for it. Therefore make hay while the sun shines. Join in with humbling providences, and do not fight against them while you+ have them (Acts 13:41). The season of grace will not last; if you+ sleep in seedtime, you+ will beg in harvest.

5. This is the way to turn humbling circumstances to good account, so that instead of being losers you+ would be gainers by them (Ps 119:71): “It was good for me to be afflicted.” Would you+ gather grapes from these thorns and thistles? Then set yourselves+ to get your+ spirits humbled by them.

(1.) Humiliation of spirit is a most valuable thing in itself (Prov 16:32). It cannot be bought too dear. Whatever one is made to suffer, if his spirit is brought down by it, he has what is well worth bearing all the hardship for (1 Pet 3:4).

(2.) Humility of spirit brings many advantages along with it. It is a fruitful bough, well loaded, wherever it is. It adds to one’s ease under the cross (Matt 11:30; Lam 3:27–29). It is a sacrifice particularly acceptable to God (Ps 51:17). The eye of God is particularly on such people for good (Isa 66:2): “This is the one I will look to: he who is humble and contrite in spirit, who trembles at My word.” Yes, he dwells with them (Isa 57:15). And it carries a line of wisdom through one’s whole conduct (Prov 11:2): “With humility comes wisdom.”

Lastly, Consider that it is a mighty hand that is at work with us, the hand of the mighty God. Let us then bend our spirits toward complying with it, and not wrestle against it. Consider:

(1.) We must fall under it. Since its design is to bring us down, we cannot stand before it, for it cannot fail in its designs (Isa 46:10): “My purpose will stand.” So fall before it we must, either in the way of duty or in the way of judgment (Ps 45:5): “Your arrows pierce the hearts of the king’s foes; the nations fall beneath your feet.”

(2.) As for those who are wise enough to fall in humiliation under the mighty hand, however low they are, the same hand will raise them up again (Jas 4:10). In a word, however high the proud are, God will bring them down. However low the humble are, God will raise them up.

Directions for reaching this humiliation.

1. General Directions.

Direction 1. Fix it in your heart to seek some spiritual profit from providence’s guidance of you (Mic 6:9). Until your heart once gets a set that way, your humiliation is not to be expected (Hos 14:9). And nothing is more reasonable, if we would act either as men or as Christians, than to aim to turn what is so grievous to the flesh to the profit of the spirit, so that if we are losers on one hand, we may be gainers on another.

2. Settle the matter of your eternal salvation in the first place, by coming to Christ and taking God for your God in him, according to the gospel offer (Hos 2:19; Heb 8:10). Let your humbling circumstances move you to this, so that while created things dry up, you may go to the Fountain. For it is impossible to reach due humiliation under the mighty hand without faith in him as your God and Friend (Heb 11:6; 1 John 4:19).

Lastly, Use the means of soul-humbling in the faith of the promise (Ps 28:7). Moses, striking the rock in the faith of the promise, made waters gush out that otherwise would not have appeared. Let us do likewise in dealing with our rocky hearts. They must be laid on the soft bed of the gospel and struck there, as in Joel 2:13, “Return to the Lord your+ God. For He is gracious and compassionate,” or they will never genuinely break or fall in humiliation.

II. Particular Directions.

1. Assure yourselves+ that there are no circumstances you+ are in so humbling but that you+ may get your+ heart acceptably brought down to them (1 Cor 10:13): “And God is faithful; He will not let you+ be tempted beyond what you+ can bear. But when you+ are tempted, He will also provide an escape, so that you+ can stand up under it.” This is the truth (2 Cor 12:9): “My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.” And you+ need to be persuaded of it, applying it to yourselves+, if ever you+ would reach the end (Phil 4:13): “I can do all things through Christ who gives me strength.” God allows you+ to be persuaded of it, whatever your+ weakness and the difficulty of the task: “This was written for us, because the plowman should plow in hope, and the thresher should thresh in hope of sharing in the harvest” (1 Cor 9:10). And believing it is a part of the life of faith (2 Tim 2:1). If you+ have no hope of success, your+ efforts will be as vain as they are dispirited. “Therefore strengthen your+ limp hands and weak knees” (Heb 12:12).

2. Whatever hand is or is not in your+ humbling circumstances, take God as the party you+ are dealing with, and consider yourselves+ in them as under his mighty hand (Mic 6:9). In their humbling circumstances men overlook God, so they do not find themselves called to humility under them. They fix their eyes on the created instrument, and instead of humility, their hearts rise. But take him as your+ party, so that you+ may remember the battle and fight no more (Job 41:8).

3. Think much of God’s infinite greatness. Consider his holiness and majesty, fit to awe you into the deepest humiliation (Isa 6:3–5). Job met with many humbling providences in his case, but he was never sufficiently humbled under them until the Lord made a new revelation of himself to him in his infinite majesty and greatness. He held his ground against his friends and stood by his points until the Lord took that method with him. It began with thunder (Job 37:1–2). Then followed God’s voice out of the whirlwind (ch. 38:1), at which Job was brought down (ch. 40:4–5). It was renewed until he was humbled further (ch. 42:5–6): “Therefore I abhor myself, and I repent in dust and ashes.”

4. Accustom yourselves+ to admit silently that there are mysteries in providence’s guidance of you+ which you+ are not able to comprehend, but which you+ will adore (Rom 11:33): “O, the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are His judgments, and untraceable His ways!” That was the first word God said to Job (ch. 38:2): “Who is this who obscures My counsel by words without knowledge?” It took him by the heart and stuck with him, and he comes back to it again (ch. 42:3) as the word that particularly brought him to his knees, to the dust. Even in those steps of providence which we seem to see far into, we may well allow that there are some mysteries beyond what we see. And in those which are perplexing and puzzling, sovereignty should silence us, and his infinite wisdom should satisfy us, though we cannot see.

5. Think much of your own sinfulness (Job 40:4): “Behold, I am vile. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth.” It is overlooking our sinfulness that gives us so much trouble with humbling circumstances. While the eyes are held so that they cannot see sin, the heart rises against these circumstances; but when the eyes are opened, the heart falls. So whenever God is dealing with you in humbling dispensations, turn your eyes, on that occasion, to the sinfulness of your nature, heart, and life, and that will help your humiliation forward.

6. Settle it in your+ heart that there is need of all the humbling circumstances you+ are put in. This is the truth (1 Pet 1:6): “though now for a little while, if need be, you+ have had to suffer grief in various trials.” God brings no needless trials on us; he afflicts none except as their need requires (Lam 3:33): “For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men.” That is a notable difference between the correction of our earthly father and that of our heavenly Father (Heb 12:10): “Our fathers disciplined us … as they thought best, but God disciplines us for our good, so that we may share in His holiness.” Look at the temper of your+ own hearts and nature: how apt they are to be lifted up, to forget God, and to be carried away with the vanities of the world; what foolishness is bound up in your+ heart. In this way you+ will see the need of humbling circumstances for ballast, and of the rod for the fool’s back. And if at any time you+ cannot see that need, believe it on the ground of God’s infinite wisdom, which does nothing in vain.

7. Believe that providence has a kind design toward you in your humbling circumstances. God calls us to this, as the key that opens the heart under them (Rev 3:19). Satan suggests suspicions to the contrary, as the bar that may hold it shut (2 Kgs 6:33): “This calamity is from the Lord. Why should I wait for the Lord any longer?” As long as suspicions of an ill design against us in them reign, the creature will, like the worm at a man’s foot, put itself in the best posture of defense it can and harden itself in sorrow. But faith in a kind design will cause it to open itself out in humility before him.

Case. “Oh! if I knew there were a kind design in it, I would willingly bear it, even if there were more of it. But I fear that providence has a ruinous design against me in it.” Answer. Now, what word of God, or what revelation from heaven, have you+ to ground these fears on? None at all; they have no ground but from hell (1 Cor 10:13). What do you+ think God’s design toward you+ in the gospel is? Can you+ believe no kind design toward you+ in all the words of grace heaped up there? What is that, I ask you+, but black unbelief in its hellish hue (Isa 55:1), flying in the face of the truth of God and making him a liar (1 John 5:10–11)? The gospel is a breathing of love and goodwill to the world of mankind-sinners (Titus 2:11 and 3:4; 1 John 4:14 and John 3:17). But in that case you+ do not believe it, any more than devils believe it. But if you+ can believe a kind design there, you+ must believe it in your+ humbling circumstances too. For the design of providence cannot be contrary to the design of the gospel; on the contrary, the latter is to help on toward the other.

8. Think to yourselves+ that this life is the time of trial for heaven (Jas 1:12): “Blessed is the man who perseveres under trial, because when he has stood the test, he will receive the crown of life that God has promised to those who love Him.” And therefore humbling circumstances should be welcomed in that light (v. 2): “Consider it pure joy … when you+ encounter trials of many kinds.” If there is an honorable office or a profitable position to be bestowed, men strive to be taken on trial for it, in the hope that they may then be lawfully admitted to it. Now God tries men for heaven by humbling circumstances, as the whole Bible teaches; and shall men be so very unwilling to stoop to them? I would ask you+:

(1.) Is it nothing to you+ to stand as a candidate for glory, to be put on trial for heaven? Is there not an honor in it, an honor all the saints have had (Jas 5:11): “See how blessed we consider those who have persevered,” etc.? And is there not a fair prospect in it (2 Cor 4:17): “For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison”? Just suppose that God should pass you+ by in that matter, as one whom it is needless ever to try on that account; that he should give you+ your+ portion in this life in full ease, as one who is to get no more from him: what would that be?

(2.) What a vast disproportion there is between your+ trials and the glory! Your+ most humbling circumstances, how light they are in comparison with the weight of it! The longest-lasting of them are but for a moment, compared with that eternal weight. Alas! there is much unbelief at the root of all our uneasiness under our humbling circumstances. If we had a clearer view of the other world, we would not make so much of either the smiles or the frowns of this one.

(3.) What do you+ think of coming off badly in the trial of your+ humbling circumstances (Jer 6:29–30)? “The bellows blow fiercely, blasting away the lead with fire. The refining proceeds in vain, for the wicked are not purged. They are called rejected silver, because the Lord has rejected them.” What if the outcome were only that your+ heart appeared to be of such a temper as by no means to be humbled, and that therefore you+ must and shall be taken out of those circumstances while still no humbling appears? I think the fearfulness of such a dispensation is enough to set us on our knees, to pray against our being lifted out of our humbling circumstances before our heart is humbled (Isa 1:5; Ezek 24:13).

9. Think to yourselves+ how it is by humbling circumstances that the Lord prepares us for heaven (Col 1:12): “giving thanks to the Father, who has made us fit to share in the inheritance of the saints in the light,” with 2 Corinthians 5:5. Stones and timber are laid down, turned over and over, and hewn before they are set up in the building; they are not simply set up as they come out of the quarry and the wood. If they were capable of choice, those of them that refused the iron tool would be refused a place in the building. Tell me, how do you+ think to be made fit for heaven by the warm sunshine of this world’s ease, and by getting all your+ will here? No, sirs, that would spoil your+ taste for the joys of the other world. Vessels of dishonor are fitted for destruction that way; but vessels of honor are fitted for glory by humbling circumstances. I would say here:

1st, Will nothing please you+ but two heavens, one here and another hereafter? God has secured one heaven for the saints, one place where they shall all have their will, wish, and desire, where there shall be no weight on them to hold them down; and that is in the other world. But you+ must have it both here and there, or you+ cannot put up with it. Why do you+ not complain too that there are not two summers in one year, or two days in the twenty-four hours? The order of the one heaven is as firm as that of the years and days, and you+ will not reverse it. Therefore choose whether you+ will take your+ night or your+ day first, your+ winter or your+ summer, your+ heaven here or hereafter.

2dly, Without being humbled by humbling circumstances in this life, you+ are not fit for heaven (2 Cor 5:5): “And God has prepared us for this very purpose.” You+ may indeed lie at ease here in a bed of sloth and dream of heaven, swollen with hopes of a fool’s paradise, wishing to throw yourselves+ straight out of Delilah’s lap into Abraham’s bosom. But unless you+ are humbled, you+ are not fit:

(1.) For the Bible heaven, the heaven described in the Old and New Testaments. Is not that heaven a lifting up in due time? But how shall you+ be lifted up who have never been properly brought down? Where will your+ tears be, to be wiped away? What place will there be for your+ triumph, if you+ will not fight the good fight? How can it be a rest to you+ who cannot bear labor?

(2.) For the saints’ heaven (Rev 7:14): “So he replied, ‘These are the ones who have come out of the great tribulation; they have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb.’” This answers the question about Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and all the saints with them there: they were brought down to the dust by humbling circumstances, and out of these they came before the throne. How can you+ ever think to be lifted up with them, when you+ cannot think of being brought down with them?

(3.) For Christ’s heaven (Heb 12:2): “who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” Oh, consider how the forerunner made his way (Luke 24:26): “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” And count on it that if you+ get where he is, you+ must go there as he went (Luke 9:23): “Then Jesus said to all of them, ‘If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross daily and follow Me.’”

10. Give up at last your+ towering hopes from this world, and confine them to the world to come. Be as pilgrims and strangers here, looking for your+ rest in heaven, and not until you+ come there. There is a prevailing evil (Isa 57:10): “You are wearied by your many journeys, but you did not say, ‘There is no hope!’” So the Babel building still goes on, though it has fallen down again and again. For men say, “The bricks have fallen, but we will rebuild with finished stone; the sycamores have been felled, but we will replace them with cedars” (Isa 9:10). This makes humbling work very long and tedious: we find it so hard to let go our grip on created things, to fall off from the breast and be weaned. But fasten your+ grip on the other world, and let your+ grip on this one go. So you+ will be humbled indeed under the mighty hand. The faster you+ grip the happiness of that world, the easier it will be to adjust yourselves+ to your+ humbling circumstances here.

Lastly, Make use of Christ in all his offices for your humiliation under your humbling circumstances. That alone is genuine humiliation which comes in that way (Zech 12:10): “They will look on Me, the One they have pierced. They will mourn,” etc. You must do this by trusting in him for that purpose:

(1.) As a priest for you. You have a conscience full of guilt, and that will make one uneasy in any circumstances, and far more in humbling circumstances; it will be like a thorn in the shoulder on which a burden is laid. But the blood of Christ will purge the conscience, draw out the thorn, and give ease (Isa 33:24), and fit for service, in doing or in suffering (Heb 9:14): “How much more will the blood of Christ … purify our consciences from works of death, so that we may serve the living God!”

(2.) As your prophet to teach you. We need to be taught to discern our humbling circumstances rightly. For we often mistake them so far that they become an oppressive load; whereas if we could see them rightly, just as God sets them before us, they would be humbling, but not so oppressive. Truly we need Christ, and the light of his word and Spirit, to let us see our cross and trial as well as our duty (Ps 25:9–10).

(3.) As your king. You have a stiff heart, unwilling to bow even in humbling circumstances. Take a lesson from Moses about what to do in such a case (Exod 34:9): “‘O Lord,’ he said, ‘… please go with us, for this is a stiff-necked people, and forgive our iniquity and sin.’” Put your heart into the hand of him who is strong and mighty (Ps 24:8). He is able to make it melt like wax before the fire, and take the impression of the seal.

Think on these directions so as to put them into practice, remembering the words, “If you+ know these things, you+ will be blessed if you+ do them.” Remember, humbling work is a work that will fill your+ hands while you+ live here, and that you+ cannot come to the end of until death; and humbling circumstances will attend you+ while you+ are in this lower world. You+ may get a change of them, but freedom from them you+ cannot get until you+ come to heaven. So the humbling circumstances of our imperfections, relationships, contradictions, afflictions, uncertainties, and sinfulness will give us matter for exercise while we are here. What remains of the purpose of this text I shall gather up in

Doctrine II.

There is a due time in which those who now humble themselves under the mighty hand of God will certainly be lifted up. We shall take:

First, A general view of this point. And consider: I. Some things supposed and implied in it. It implies:

1. That those who shall share in his lifting up must reckon, in the first place, on a casting down (Rev 7:14; John 16:33): “In the world you+ will have tribulation.” According to the settled method of grace, there is no coming to the promised land except through the wilderness, nor entering into this exaltation except through a narrow gate. If we cannot bear casting down, we will not taste the sweetness of the lifting up.

2. Being cast down by the mighty hand of God, we must learn to lie still and quiet under it until the same hand that cast us down raises us up, if we would share in this promised lifting up (Lam 3:27). It is not being cast down into humbling circumstances by the providence of God, but the coming down of our spirits under them by the grace of God, that brings us within the reach of this promise.

3. Never humbled in humbling circumstances, never lifted up in the way of this promise. Men may keep their spirits high and unbent in their humbling circumstances, and in that case may get a lifting up (Prov 16:19). But note this: what they get will be a lifting up to the end that they may have the more grievous fall. “Surely You set them on slick ground; You cast them down into ruin” (Ps 73:18). But those who will not humble themselves in humbling circumstances will find their obstinacy a clinching nail, which will keep their misery fast on them forever without remedy.

4. Humility of spirit in humbling circumstances makes certain a lifting up out of them at some time, with the goodwill and favor of Heaven (Luke 18:14): “I tell you, this man, rather than the Pharisee, went home justified. For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but the one who humbles himself will be exalted.” Solomon observes (Prov 15:1) that “a gentle answer turns away wrath, but a harsh word stirs up anger.” And so it is that while the proud, by their obstinacy, only twist the yoke tighter around their own necks, the yielding humble ones make their relief sure by their very yielding (1 Sam 2:8–10): “He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap. He seats them among princes and bestows on them a throne of honor. … He guards the steps of His faithful ones, but the wicked perish in darkness; for by his own strength shall no man prevail. Those who oppose the Lord will be shattered.” So the cannonball breaks down a stone wall, while yielding packs of wool take away its force.

5. There is an appointed time for the lifting up of those who humble themselves in their humbling circumstances (Hab 2:3): “For the vision awaits an appointed time; it testifies of the end and does not lie. Though it lingers, wait for it, since it will surely come and will not tarry.” There is a time for everything, for humbling as well as for lifting up (Eccl 3:3). We do not know it, but God knows it, for he has appointed it. Let not the humble one say, “I will never be lifted up.” There is a time fixed for it, as precisely as for the rising of the sun after the long, dark night, or the return of spring after the long, sharp winter.

6. It is not to be expected that the lifting up will follow immediately when one humbles himself. No, one is not only to lie down under the mighty hand, but to lie still, waiting for the due time. Humbling work is long work: the Israelites had forty years of it in the wilderness. God’s people must be brought to put a blank in his hand as to the time, and while they have a long night of walking in darkness, they must trust: “Who among you+ fears the Lord and obeys the voice of His Servant? Who among you+ walks in darkness and has no light? Let him trust in the name of the Lord let him lean on his God” (Isa 50:10).

7. The appointed time for the lifting up is the due time, the time fittest for it, in which it will come most seasonably: “Let us not grow weary in well-doing, for in due time we will reap a harvest if we do not give up” (Gal 6:9). For that is the time God has chosen for it, and be sure that his choice, as the choice of infinite wisdom, is the best. And therefore faith sets itself to wait for it: “The one who believes will not make haste” (Isa 28:16). Much of the beauty of a thing depends on its timing, and he has fixed that in all he does: “He has made everything beautiful in its time” (Eccl 3:11).

Lastly, The lifting up of the humbled will not fail to come in the appointed and due time (Hab 2:3). Time makes no halt; it is running day and night. So the due time is fast coming, and when it comes, it will bring the lifting up along with it. Let the humbling circumstances be ever so low, ever so hopeless, it is impossible that the lifting up from them should not come in the due time.

II. A word in general on the lifting up that awaits those who humble themselves. There is a twofold lifting up.

1. A partial lifting up, which belongs to the humbled in time, during this life: “I will exalt You, O Lord, for You have lifted me up and have not allowed my foes to rejoice over me” (Ps 30:1). This is a lifting up in part, and only in part, not wholly. Such liftings up the humbled may expect while in this world, but no more. These give the weary a breathing space and a change of burdens, but do not set them perfectly at ease. So Israel in the wilderness, in the midst of their many times of mourning, had some times of singing (Exod 15:1; Num 21:17).

2. A total lifting up, which belongs to them at the end of time, at death: “One day the beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side” (Luke 16:22). Then the Lord deals with them no more by pieces and halves, but carries their relief to perfection (Heb 12:23). Then he takes off all their burdens, eases them of all their weights, and lays no more on them forever. He then lifts them up to a height they were never at before, no, not even when at their highest. He sets them quite above all that is low, and fixes them there, never to be brought down again. Now there is a due time for both of these.

1. For the partial lifting up. Not every time is fit for it; we are not always fit to receive comfort, an ease or a change of our burdens. God sees that there are times when it is needful for his people to be in heaviness (1 Pet 1:6), and to have their hearts brought down with grief (Ps 107:12). But then there is a time really appointed for it in the divine wisdom, when he will think it as needful to comfort them as he did before to bring them down: “So instead, you+ ought to forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow” (2 Cor 2:7). In that case we are in the hand of God as in the hand of our physician. He appoints how long the drawing plaster is to lie on, and when the healing plaster is to be applied, and does not leave it to the patient.

2. For the total lifting up. When we are sorely oppressed with our burdens, we are ready to think, O to be away, and set beyond them all! (Job 7:2–3): “Like a slave he longs for shade; like a hireling he waits for his wages. So I am allotted months of futility, and nights of misery are appointed me.” But for all that, it may be fitter that we stay a while and wrestle with our burdens: “But it is more necessary for you+ that I remain in the body. Convinced of this, I know that I will remain and will continue with all of you+ for your+ progress and joy in the faith” (Phil 1:24–25). A few days might have taken Israel out of Egypt into Canaan; but they would have been there too soon if they had made all that speed. So they had to spend forty years in the wilderness, until their due time of entering Canaan should come. And be sure that the saints, on entering heaven, will be convinced that its time was best chosen, and that there is a beauty in its coming no sooner.

And so a lifting up is secured to the humble.

III. The certainty of the lifting up of those who humble themselves under humbling circumstances. If someone were to assure you+, when you+ were reduced to poverty, that the time would certainly yet come when you+ would be rich; or, when you+ were very sick, that you+ would not die of that disease but would certainly recover, that would help you+ to bear your+ poverty and sickness better. And you+ would comfort yourselves+ with that prospect. One may, however, stay poor and never be rich; one may be sick and die of his disease. But as for all who humble themselves under their humbling circumstances, we can assure them from the Lord’s word that they will certainly, beyond all doubt, be lifted up out of their humbling circumstances and relieved from them. They will certainly see the day of their ease and relief, when they will remember their burdens as waters that have dried up. And you+ may be assured of this from the following considerations.

1st, The nature of God, duly considered, ensures it: “The Lord is compassionate and gracious, slow to anger, abounding in loving devotion. He will not always accuse us, nor harbor His anger forever” (Ps 103:8–9). The humbled soul, looking to God in Christ, may see three things in his nature that together secure it.

1. Infinite power, which can do all things. No circumstances are so low that he cannot raise them, none so entangling and perplexing that he cannot unravel them, none so hopeless that he cannot remedy them: “Is anything too difficult for the Lord?” (Gen 18:14). Whatever our case may be, it is never past his reach to help it. Indeed, the most proper season for him to take it in hand is when all others have given it up: “For the Lord will vindicate His people and have compassion on His servants when He sees that their strength is gone and no one remains, slave or free” (Deut 32:36).

2. Infinite goodness, inclining him to help. He is good and gracious in his nature (Exod 34:6–9), and therefore his power is a spring of comfort to them (Rom 14:4). Men may be willing who are not able, or able who are not willing. But infinite goodness joined with infinite power in God may assure the humbled of a lifting up in due time. That is a word of inconceivable sweetness: “And we have come to know and believe the love that God has for us. God is love; whoever abides in love abides in God, and God in him” (1 John 4:16). He has the tender heart of a Father toward the humble: “As a father has compassion on his children, so the Lord has compassion on those who fear Him” (Ps 103:13). Yes, he has tender mercies, more tender than a mother’s to her nursing child (Isa 49:15). Therefore, although his wisdom may see it necessary to put them in humbling circumstances and keep them there for a time, it is not possible that he should leave them in them altogether.

3. Infinite wisdom, which does nothing in vain, and therefore will not needlessly keep anyone in humbling circumstances: “Even if He causes grief, He will show compassion according to His abundant loving devotion. For He does not willingly afflict or grieve the sons of men” (Lam 3:32–33). God sends these circumstances on them for humbling, as the end and design to be brought about by them. When that is obtained, and there is no more use for them in that way, we may be sure they will be taken off.

2dly, The providence of God, viewed in its settled methods of proceeding with its objects, ensures it. Turn your+ eyes whichever way you+ will on the divine providence, and you+ may conclude from it that in due time the humble will be lifted up.

1. Observe the providence of God in the turns of the whole course of nature: day following the longest night, summer following winter, the waxing of the moon following its waning, the flowing of the sea following its ebbing, and so on. Let not the Lord’s humbled ones be idle spectators of these things; they are for our learning: “Thus says the Lord, who gives the sun for light by day, who sets in order the moon and stars for light by night, who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar—the Lord of Hosts is His name: ‘Only if this fixed order departed from My presence, declares the Lord, would Israel’s descendants ever cease to be a nation before Me’” (Jer 31:35–37). Will the Lord’s hand keep such a steady course in the earth, the sea and the visible heavens as to bring a lifting up in them after a casting down, and forget only his humbled ones? No.

2. Observe the providence of God in its dealings with the man Christ, its most noble and majestic object, more valuable than a thousand worlds (Col 2:9). Did not providence keep this course with him, first humbling him, then exalting him and lifting him up? Did it not first bring him to the dust of death, in a course of sufferings for thirty-three years, and then exalt him to the Father’s right hand in an eternity of glory? “who for the joy set before Him endured the cross, scorning its shame, and sat down at the right hand of the throne of God” (Heb 12:2). “And being found in appearance as a man, He humbled Himself and became obedient to death—even death on a cross. Therefore God exalted Him to the highest place” (Phil 2:8–9). The exaltation could not fail to follow his humiliation: “Was it not necessary for the Christ to suffer these things and then to enter His glory?” (Luke 24:26). And he saw and believed that it would follow, as the springing up of the seed follows its sowing (John 12:24). The humbled in humbling circumstances have a close concern in this.

(1.) This is the pattern providence copies in its guidance of you+. The Father was so well pleased with this method in the case of his own Son that it was determined to be followed, and copied over again exactly, in the case of all the heirs of glory: “For those God foreknew, He also predestined to be conformed to the image of His Son, so that He would be the firstborn among many brothers” (Rom 8:29). And who will not be pleased to walk through the darkest valley, treading in his steps?

(2.) This is a sure pledge of your+ lifting up. Christ in his state of humiliation was considered as a public person and representative, and so he is in his exaltation. So Christ’s exaltation ensures your+ exaltation out of your+ humbling circumstances: “Your dead will live; together with my dead body they will rise. Awake and sing, you+ who dwell in the dust!” (Isa 26:19). “Come, let us return to the Lord. For He has torn us to pieces, but He will heal us; He has wounded us, but He will bind up our wounds. After two days He will revive us; on the third day He will raise us up, that we may live in His presence” (Hos 6:1–2). “And God raised us up with Christ and seated us with Him in the heavenly realms in Christ Jesus” (Eph 2:6). Yes, he has gone into the state of glory for us, as our forerunner: “where Jesus our forerunner has entered on our behalf. He has become a high priest forever” (Heb 6:20).

(3.) His humiliation was the price of our exaltation, and his exaltation is a full testimony that the payment was accepted in full. There are no humbling circumstances you+ are in but you+ would have perished in them, had he not purchased your+ lifting up out of them by his own humiliation (Isa 26:19). Now his humbling grace in you+ is evidence that his humiliation is accepted for your+ lifting up.

3. Observe the providence of God toward the church in all ages. This has been the course the Lord has kept with her (Ps 129:1–4). Abel was slain by wicked Cain, to the great grief of Adam and Eve and the rest of their godly children; but then another seed was raised up afterward in Abel’s place (Gen 4:25). Noah and his sons were buried alive in the ark for more than a year; but then they were brought out into a new world and blessed. Abraham went childless for many years; but at length Isaac was born. Israel was long in miserable bondage in Egypt; but at length they were settled in the promised land, and so on. We must be content to go by the footsteps of the flock; and if we follow them in humiliation, we will surely follow them in exaltation too.

4. Observe the providence of God in the dealings of his grace with his children. The general rule is: “God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Pet 5:5). How are they brought into a state of grace? Is it not by a sound work of humiliation going before (Luke 6:48)? And ordinarily, the greater the measure of grace designed for someone, the deeper is their humiliation beforehand, as in Paul’s case. If they are to be recovered out of a backslidden condition, the same method is followed. So the deepest humiliations ordinarily make way for the greatest comforts, and the darkest hour comes before the rising of the Sun of righteousness on them (Isa 66:5–13).

Lastly, Observe the providence of God at length throwing down wicked men, however long they stand and prosper: “I have seen a wicked, ruthless man flourishing like a green, well-rooted native tree, yet he passed away and was no more; though I searched, he could not be found” (Ps 37:35–36). They are long green before the sun, but at length they are suddenly struck with an east wind and wither away. Their lamp goes out with a stench, and they are put out in utter darkness. Now it is inconsistent with the kindness of the divine nature to forget to raise the humble while he remembers to bring down the proud.

3dly, The word of God puts it beyond all doubt. From beginning to end it is the humbled saint’s security for a lifting up: “Remember Your word to Your servant, upon which You have given me hope. This is my comfort in affliction, that Your promise has given me life” (Ps 119:49–50). His word is the great letter of his name, which he will certainly cause to shine: “You have exalted Your word above all Your name” (Ps 138:2). And in all generations it has been safely trusted (Ps 12:6). Consider:

1. The doctrines of the word, which teach faith and hope for the time, and the happy outcome the exercise of these graces will have. The whole current of Scripture to those in humbling circumstances is “not to throw away their confidence, but to hope to the end,” and that for this good reason, that “it will not be in vain.” See Ps 27:14: “Wait patiently for the Lord be strong and courageous, and He will strengthen your heart. Wait patiently for the Lord!” And compare Rom 9:33 and Isa 49:23: “Those who wait for Me will never be put to shame.”

2. The promises of the word, by which Heaven is expressly pledged to give a lifting up to those who humble themselves in humbling circumstances: “Humble yourselves+ before the Lord, and He will exalt you+” (Jas 4:10). “Whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Matt 23:12). It may take time to prepare them for lifting up, but once that is done, it is secured: “You have heard, O Lord, the desire of the humble; You will prepare their hearts. You will incline Your ear” (Ps 10:17). They have his word for deliverance (Ps 50:15). And though they may seem to be forgotten, they will not always be so; the time of their deliverance will come: “For the needy will not always be forgotten; nor the hope of the oppressed forever dashed” (Ps 9:18). “He will turn toward the prayer of the destitute; He will not despise their prayer” (Ps 102:17).

3. The examples of the word, which sufficiently confirm the truth of the doctrines and promises: “For everything that was written in the past was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and the encouragement of the Scriptures, we might have hope” (Rom 15:4). In the doctrines and promises the lifting up is set before our faith, to be counted on, on the strength of God’s word. But in the examples it is set before our eyes, in the case of others, to be seen: “See how blessed we consider those who have persevered. You+ have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy” (Jas 5:11). There we see it in the case of Abraham, Job, David, Paul and other saints; but above all, in the case of the man Christ.

Lastly, The intercession of Christ, joined with the prayers and cries of his humbled people in their humbling circumstances, ensures a lifting up for them at length. Granted that the proud do not cry when he binds them, yet his own humbled ones will not be like them; they will cry: “Deep calls to deep in the roar of Your waterfalls; all Your breakers and waves have rolled over me. The Lord decrees His loving devotion by day, and at night His song is with me as a prayer to the God of my life” (Ps 42:7–8). And though unbelievers may soon be wearied out and give it up altogether, true believers will not. Though they may, in a fit of temptation, lay it aside as hopeless, they will find themselves obliged to take it up again: “If I say, ‘I will not mention Him or speak any more in His name,’ His message becomes a fire burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail” (Jer 20:9). And they will continue to cry night and day (Luke 18:7), knowing no time for giving it up until they are lifted up: “My eyes overflow unceasingly, without relief, until the Lord looks down from heaven and sees” (Lam 3:49–50). Now since Christ’s intercession is joined with these cries, there cannot fail to be a lifting up. Consider:

1. Christ’s intercession is certainly joined with the cries and prayers of the humbled in their humbling circumstances: “Then another angel, who had a golden censer, came and stood at the altar. He was given much incense to offer, along with the prayers of all the saints, on the golden altar before the throne” (Rev 8:3). They are helped by the Spirit to groan for relief (Rom 8:26), and the prayers and groans that are through the Spirit are certain to be made effectual by the intercession of the Son (Jas 5:16). And you+ may know they are by the Spirit if you+ are helped to continue praying, hoping for your+ suit to be granted at last on the ground of God’s word of promise. For nature’s praying is a pool that will dry up in a long drought; it is the spirit of prayer that is the lasting spring (John 4:14). “On the day I called, You answered me; You emboldened me and strengthened my soul” (Ps 138:3). Truly there is an intercession in heaven on account of the humbling circumstances of the humble ones: “Then the angel of the Lord said, ‘How long, O Lord of Hosts, will You withhold mercy from Jerusalem and the cities of Judah, with which You have been angry these seventy years?’” (Zech 1:12). How then can they fail of a lifting up in due time?

2. He is in deep earnest in his intercession for his people in their humbling circumstances. Some will speak a good word for the helpless and yet care little whether they succeed or not. But our Intercessor is in earnest on behalf of his humbled ones, for he is touched with sympathy in their case: “In all their distress, He too was afflicted” (Isa 63:9). It is a most tender sympathy: “For whoever touches you+ touches the apple of His eye” (Zech 2:8). He has their case on his heart where he is, in the holy place in the highest heavens (Exod 28:29), and he keeps an exact account of the time of their humbling circumstances, however long it may be (Zech 1:12). Moreover, it is his own business. The lifting up they are to have is a thing secured to him in the promises made to him on account of his shedding his blood for them (Ps 89:33, 36). So not only are they looking for it on earth, but the man Christ is in heaven looking for the fulfillment of these promises: “But when this Priest had offered for all time one sacrifice for sins, He sat down at the right hand of God. Since that time, He waits expectantly for His enemies to be made a footstool for His feet” (Heb 10:12–13). How is it possible, then, that this looking should be disappointed? Moreover, these humbling circumstances are still his own sufferings, though not in his person, yet in his members: “Now I rejoice in my sufferings for you+, and I fill up in my flesh what is lacking in regard to Christ’s afflictions for the sake of His body, which is the church” (Col 1:24). Therefore there is every ground to conclude that he is in deep earnest.

Lastly, His intercession is always effectual: “I knew that You always hear Me” (John 11:42). It cannot fail to be so, because he is the Father’s well-beloved Son, and his intercession has a plea of justice for its ground: “We have an advocate before the Father—Jesus Christ, the Righteous One” (1 John 2:1). Moreover, he has all power in heaven and earth lodged in him (John 5:22). And finally, he and his Father are one, and their will is one. So, for the present time, both Christ and his Father do will the lifting up of the humbled ones, but only in the due time.

Secondly, I go on to a more particular view of the point. And:

I. We will consider the lifting up as brought about in time, which is the partial lifting up. And:

First, Some considerations for clearing up its nature.

1. This lifting up does not take place in every case of a child of God. One may be humbled in humbling circumstances from which he is not to get a lifting up in time. We should not at once conclude from the promise that, being humbled under our humbling circumstances, we will certainly be taken out of them and freed from them before we come to the end of our journey. For it is certain that there are some circumstances, such as our imperfections, our sinfulness and our mortality, that we can by no means be rid of while in this world. And there are particular humbling circumstances the Lord may hang about one man and keep about him till he goes down to the grave, while in the meantime he may lift up another from the same. Heman was pressed down all along from his youth (Ps 88:15); others, all their lifetime (Heb 2:15).

Objection. If that is the case, what becomes of the promise of lifting up? Where is the lifting up, if one may go to the grave under the weight? Answer. If there were no life after this, there would be weight in that objection; but since there is another life, there is no weight in it at all. In the other life the promise will be fulfilled to the humbled, as it was to Lazarus (Luke 16:22). Consider that the great appointed time for fulfilling the promises is the other life, not this one: “All these people died in faith, without having received the promises. However, they saw them and welcomed them from afar” (Heb 11:13). And consider that whatever fulfillment of the promise there is here, it is not of the nature of the stock itself, but of a sample or a pledge.

Question. But then, may we not give up praying for the lifting up in that case? Answer. We do not know when that is our case. For a case may be past all hope in our eyes, and in the eyes of others, in which God still designs a lifting up in time, as in Job’s: “What strength do I have, that I should still hope? What is my future, that I should be patient?” (Job 6:11). But be that as it may, we should never give up praying for the lifting up, since it will certainly come to all who pray for it in faith; if not here, then hereafter. The promise is sure, and to pray is the commandment. So such praying cannot fail of a happy outcome at length: “Call upon Me in the day of trouble; I will deliver you, and you will honor Me” (Ps 50:15). The whole life of a Christian is such a praying, waiting life, and all temporal deliverances are given as pledges to encourage it: “Not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit, groan inwardly as we wait eagerly for our adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Rom 8:23). And whoever observes that the full lifting up at death is at hand must certainly take heart again, even if he has given up his case as hopeless.

2. However, there are some cases in which this lifting up does take place. God gives his people some notable liftings up even in time, raising them out of remarkable humbling circumstances. The storm is changed into a calm, and they remember it as waters that have dried up (Ps 40:1–4). Two things may be observed on this.

(1.) One may be in humbling circumstances very long, sore and hopeless, and yet a lifting up of much longer continuance may be awaiting him. This is sometimes the case of the children of God who are set to bear the yoke in their youth, as it was with Joseph and David. It is sometimes the case of those who have it laid on them in their middle age, as it was with Job, who could not have been less than forty when his trouble came, but after it lived a hundred and forty years (Job 42:16). By such methods God prepares men for special usefulness.

(2.) One may be in humbling circumstances long and sore, and quite hopeless in the ordinary course of providence, and yet they may get a clear and warm gleam of a lifting up before they come to their journey’s end. The life of some of God’s children is like a cloudy and rainy day, in which, in the evening, the sun breaks out from under the clouds, shines fair and clear for a little while, and then sets: “On that day the light will be neither clear nor dark … but when evening comes, there will be light” (Zech 14:6–7). Such was the case of Jacob in his old age: he was brought with honor and comfort to Egypt, to his son, and then he died.

(3.) Yet whatever liftings up they get in this life, they will never be without some weights hanging about them for their humbling. They may have their singing times, but their songs, while in this world, will be mixed with groanings: “So while we are in this tent, we groan under our burdens” (2 Cor 5:4). The unmixed dispensation is reserved for the other world; this one will be a wilderness to the end, where there will be howlings with the most joyful notes.

Lastly, All the liftings up the humbled meet with now are pledges, and only pledges, samples and an earnest of the great lifting up awaiting them on the other side; and they should look on them so.

(1.) They are really so: “There I will give back her vineyards and make the Valley of Achor into a gateway of hope. There she will respond as she did in the days of her youth, as in the day she came up out of Egypt” (Hos 2:15). Our Lord Jesus is now leading his people through the wilderness, and the manna and the water from the rock are an earnest of the time of the milk and honey flowing in the promised land. They have not yet come home to their Father’s house, but they are traveling on the road, and Christ their elder brother is with them (Song 4:8). He bears their expenses, takes them into inns by the way, as it were, and refreshes them with partial liftings up, after which they must take to the road again. But that hospitality by the way is a pledge of the full hospitality he will give them when they have come home.

Objection. But people may get a lifting up in time that is still no pledge of a lifting up on the other side. How then shall I know it to be a pledge? Answer. That lifting up which comes by the promise is certainly a pledge of the full lifting up in the other world. For as the other life is the proper time for fulfilling the promises, so we may be sure that when God once begins to clear his bond, he will certainly hold on till it is fully cleared: “The Lord will perfect what concerns me” (Ps 138:8). So we may say, as Naomi said to Ruth on her receiving the six measures of barley from Boaz, “He will not rest unless he has resolved the matter today” (Ruth 3:18). There are liftings up that come by common providence, and these indeed are single, and not pledges of more. But the promise chains mercies together, so that one received is a pledge of another to come, yes, of the whole chain to the end (2 Sam 5:12).

Question. But how shall I know that the lifting up comes by way of the promise? That which comes by way of the promise comes at the same time by the low way of humiliation, the high way of faith, or believing the promise, and the long way of waiting hope and patient continuance: “Be patient, then, brothers, until the Lord’s coming. See how the farmer awaits the precious fruit of the soil—how patient he is for the fall and spring rains” (Jas 5:7). Humility qualifies for the fulfillment of the promise; faith sucks the breast of it; and patient waiting hangs on the breast till the milk comes abundantly.

(2.) But no liftings up of God’s children here are any more than pledges of lifting up. God gives worldly men their stock here, but his children get nothing here but a sample of theirs (Ps 17:14), just as the servant gets his wages in one sum on payday, while the young heir gets nothing but a few pennies for spending money. The truth is, this same spending money is more valuable than the world’s stock: “You have filled my heart with more joy than when grain and new wine abound” (Ps 4:7). But though it is better than the world’s stock, and better than their own services too, and worth more than all their waiting on him, yet it is below the honor of their God to put them off with it: “Instead, they were longing for a better country, a heavenly one. Therefore God is not ashamed to be called their God, for He has prepared a city for them” (Heb 11:16).

Secondly, The partial lifting up itself: what they will get in getting this lifting up promised to the humbled. Why, they will get:

1. A removal of their humbling circumstances. God, having tried them a while, and humbled them, and brought down their hearts, will at length take off their burden. He will remove the weight that has hung on them so long, and so bring them joyfully off that part of their trial, and let them straighten their backs that have long been bowed down. And this he does in one of two ways.

(1.) Either in kind, removing the burden for good and all. Such a lifting up Job got when the Lord turned back his captivity and increased again his family and his possessions, both of which had been laid waste. So did David, when Saul his persecutor fell in battle and David was brought to the kingdom, after many weary days of expecting one day to fall by Saul’s hand. It is easy for our God to make such turns in the most humbling circumstances.

(2.) Or in an equivalent, or as good, removing the weight of the burden, so that though the burden remains, it presses them no more: “But He said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness.’ Therefore I will boast all the more gladly in my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may rest on me. That is why, for the sake of Christ, I delight in weaknesses” (2 Cor 12:9–10). Though they have not reached the shore, yet their head is no longer under the water, but lifted up. David speaks feelingly of such a lifting up: “For in the day of trouble He will hide me in His shelter; He will conceal me under the cover of His tent; He will set me high upon a rock. Then my head will be lifted up above my enemies around me. At His tabernacle I will offer sacrifices with shouts of joy; I will sing and make music to the Lord” (Ps 27:5–6). Such a lifting up the three young men had in the fiery furnace: the fire burned, but it could burn nothing of them but their bonds; they had its warmth and light, but nothing of its scorching heat. Sometimes God lifts up his people in this way in their humbling circumstances.

2. A comforting sight of the acceptance of the prayers they put up in their humbling circumstances. While prayers are not answered, but trouble continues, those who wait on at the Lord’s hand are apt to think they are not accepted or regarded in heaven, because there is no change in their case: “If I summoned Him and He answered me, I do not believe He would listen to my voice. For He would crush me with a tempest” (Job 9:16–17). But that is a mistake. They are accepted at once, though not answered: “And this is the confidence that we have before Him: If we ask anything according to His will, He hears us” (1 John 5:14). The Lord does with them as a father does with the letters coming thick from his son abroad: he reads them one by one with pleasure, and carefully lays them up to be answered at his convenience. And when the answer comes, the son will know how acceptable they were to his father (Matt 15:28). So, etc.

3. A heart-satisfying answer to these prayers (ibid. [in the same place]), so that they will not only get the thing, but see that they have it as an answer to prayer; and they will put a double value on the mercy (1 Sam 2:1). Accepted prayers may be very long in being answered, many years, as in the case of Abraham and of David, but they cannot fail of an answer at length (Ps 9:18). The time will come when God will count it out to them according to the promise, so that they will change their note and say, “I love the Lord, for He has heard my voice—my appeal for mercy” (Ps 116:1). They will look on their lifting up as bearing the signature of the hand of a prayer-hearing God.

4. Full satisfaction as to the guidance of providence in all the steps of the humbling circumstances, and in the delay of the lifting up, however perplexing these were before (Rev 15:3). Standing on the shore and looking back on what they have passed through, they will be made to say, “He has done all things well.” The things that are bitter to Christians in passing through them are very sweet when they look back on them. So Samson’s riddle is proved true in their experience.

5. They get the lifting up together with the interest for the time they were kept out of it. When God pays his bonds of promise, he pays both principal and interest together: the mercy is increased according to the time the man waited, and to the expenses and hardships he bore while the case was pending. The fruits of common providence are soon ripe and soon rotten; but the fruit of the promise is usually long in ripening, but then it is durable; and the longer it is in ripening, the more valuable it is when it comes. Abraham and Sarah waited for the promise about ten years. At length they thought of a way to hasten it (Gen 16), which soon brought about the birth of Ishmael; but he was not the promised son. They were coming into extreme old age before the promise brought forth (Gen 18:11). But when it came, they got it with an addition, the renewing of their age (Gen 21:7; 25:1). The most valuable of all the promises, that is, the promise of Christ, was the longest in fulfilling: it took four thousand years.

Lastly, The spiritual enemies that flew thick and fast about them in the time of the darkness of their humbling circumstances will be scattered at this lifting up in the promise: “At that time Hannah prayed: ‘My heart rejoices in the Lord … My mouth speaks boldly against my enemies … The well-fed hire themselves out for food, but the starving hunger no more’” (1 Sam 2:1, 5). Pharaoh’s army behind the Israelites was formidable while they had the Red Sea before them; but when they were through the sea, they saw the Egyptians dead on the shore (Exod 14:30). Such a sight of their spiritual enemies will those who humble themselves under humbling circumstances get, when the time comes for their lifting up.

Thirdly, The due time of this lifting up. That is a natural question for those in humbling circumstances: “Watchman, what is left of the night?” And we cannot answer it to the humbled soul except in general (Isa 21:11–12). So take these general observations on it.

1. The lifting up of the humbled will not be long in coming, considering the weight of the matter. That is to say, considering the worth and value of the lifting up of the humble, when it comes, the time it took can by no means be reckoned long. When you+ sow your+ grain in the fields, though it does not ripen as soon as some garden seeds, but you+ wait three months or so, you+ do not think the harvest long in coming, considering the value of the crop. This is the view the apostle takes of the lifting up in humbling circumstances: “For our light and momentary affliction is producing for us an eternal weight of glory that is far beyond comparison” (2 Cor 4:17). So a believer, looking on the promise with an eye of faith, and seeing its fulfillment and the work it does when fulfilled, may wonder that it has come after so short a waiting. Therefore it is declared to be a time that comes soon (Luke 18:8): soon in respect of its weight and worth.

2. When the time comes, it, and it only, will appear to be the due time. To everything there is a season, and a great part of wisdom lies in discerning it and doing things in their season. And we may be sure that infinite wisdom cannot miss the season by mistaking it: “He is the Rock, His work is perfect; all His ways are just” (Deut 32:4). Indeed, whatever God does will stand the strictest examination in this as in every other point: “I know that everything God does endures forever; nothing can be added to it or taken from it. God does it so that they should fear Him” (Eccl 3:14). It is true that many seasons present themselves to us as the due time for lifting up which really are not so, because some circumstance is hidden from us that makes that season unfit for the thing. Hence John 7:6: “Although your time is always at hand, My time has not yet come.” But when all the circumstances, always foreknown by God, come to be unfolded and laid together before us, we will then see that the lifting up came in the nick of time, most for the honor of God and our good, and that it would not have done so well sooner.

3. When the time comes that is really the due time, the proper time for lifting up a child of God from his humbling circumstances, it will not be put off one moment longer: “At the end it will speak … it will surely come and will not tarry” (Hab 2:3). Though it tarries, it will not linger or be put off to another time. O what rest of heart the firm faith of this would give us! There is not a child of God who would not, with the utmost care, protest against a lifting up before the due time, as against unripe fruit thrown to him by an angry father, which would set his teeth on edge. Since it is so, then, if we could firmly believe this point, that it will undoubtedly come in the due time without the loss of a minute, it would give us sound rest. It must be so, because God has said it. Were the case ever so hopeless, and were mountains of difficulties lying in its way, at the appointed time it will “blow,” as the Hebrew has it (Hab 2:3): a metaphor from the wind rising in a moment after a dead calm.

4. The humbling circumstances are ordinarily carried to the utmost point of hopelessness before the lifting up. The knife was at Isaac’s throat before the voice was heard. “We do not want you+ to be unaware, brothers, of the hardships we encountered in the province of Asia. We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life. Indeed, we felt we were under the sentence of death, in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor 1:8–9). Things soon seem to us to have arrived at that point; such is the hastiness of our spirits. But things may have far to go down after we think they are at the foot of the hill. And we are almost as poor judges of the point of hopelessness as of the due time of lifting up. But usually God carries his people’s humbling circumstances downward, downward, still downward, till they come to that point. Two reasons for this are to be noticed.

(1.) One from the exemplary cause of it. In this God is holding the same course he held in the case of the man Christ, the beloved pattern copied in all the dealings of providence with the church and with every particular believer (Rom 8:29). He was a man of sorrows all along. As his time went on, the waters swelled more, till he was brought to the dust of death. Then he was buried, and the gravestone sealed. When that was done, the world thought they were wholly rid of him, and that he would trouble them no more. But they were quite mistaken: then, and not till then, was the due time of lifting him up. And the most remarkable liftings up that his people get are only little pieces fashioned after this grand pattern.

(2.) Another from the final cause, the end and design providence aims at in it. That is, to carry the believer clean off all foundations of his own, and off all created foundations, so that he rests his trust and hope on the Lord alone: “in order that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead” (2 Cor 1:9). The life of a Christian here is designed to be a life of faith. And though faith may act more easily when it has some help from sight, yet it certainly acts most nobly when it acts in the very face of sight. Then it is pure faith, when it stands only on its own native legs, the power and word of God: “Without weakening in his faith, he did not consider his own body, now as good as dead … nor the lifelessness of Sarah’s womb. He did not waver through disbelief in the promise of God, but was strengthened in his faith and gave glory to God” (Rom 4:19–20). And this is what faith must do when the matter is carried to the utmost point of hopelessness.

Lastly, Due preparation of the heart for the lifting up out of the humbling circumstances goes before the due time of that lifting up according to the promise. It is not so in every lifting up. The liftings up of common providence are not so exactly managed. Men will have them and will not do without them any longer, and God flings them to them in anger before they are prepared for them: “So in My anger I gave you a king” (Hos 13:11). They can by no means stand the trial, and God takes them off the fire as reprobate silver that cannot stand it (Jer 6:29–30).

This due preparation consists in due humiliation (Ps 10:17). And it often takes much work to bring this about, which is another point we are very poor judges of. We would have thought Job was brought very low in his spirit by the providence of God bruising him on the one hand, and his friends on the other, for a long time. Yet after all he had endured both ways, God saw it necessary to speak to him himself for his humiliation (Job 38:1). By that speech of God himself he was brought to his knees (Job 40:4–5). And we would have thought he was then sufficiently humbled, and perhaps he thought so himself too. But God saw a further degree of humiliation to be necessary, and therefore began to speak anew for his humiliation, which at length laid him in the dust (Job 42:5–6). And when he was thus prepared for lifting up, he got it.

There are six things, I think, that belong to this humiliation which prepares for lifting up.

1. A deep sense of sinfulness, and of unworthiness of being lifted up at all: “Behold, I am vile. How can I reply to You? I place my hand over my mouth” (Job 40:4). People may be long in humbling circumstances before they are brought this far. Even good men are biased in their own favor, and may so far forget themselves as to think that God deals out his favors unequally and is very severe on them beyond others. Elihu notes this wrong in Job under his humbling circumstances (Job 33:10–12). And I believe it will be found that there is usually a greater keenness to vindicate our own honor from the charge the humbling circumstances seem to lay on it than to vindicate the honor of God in the justice and fairness of the dispensation. The blindness of an ill-natured world, always ready to suspect the worst causes for humbling circumstances, as if the greatest sufferers were surely the greatest sinners (Luke 13:4), gives a handle to this bias of corrupt nature. But God is a jealous God, and when he comes forward to humble sufficiently, he will make the matter of our honor give way like a sandy bank under our feet, while we will be obliged to grasp hastily at the vindication of his.

2. A resignation to the divine pleasure as to the time of lifting up. God gives the promise, leaving the time blank as far as we are concerned. Our time is always at hand, and we rashly fill it in on our own authority. God does not keep our time, because it is not the due time. Hence we are ready to think his word fails, whereas it is only our own rash conclusion from it that fails: “In my haste I said, ‘All men are liars!’” (Ps 116:11). Several of the saints have had their fingers rapped this way, and so learned to leave off filling in that blank.
