The first promise was treated so by believing Eve (Gen 4:1); another promise by believing Abraham, after waiting about ten years (Gen 16); another by David, cited above (Ps 116:11).

If this is the case of any child of God, let them not be discouraged by it, thinking they were over-rash in applying the promise to themselves. They were rash only in applying the time to the promise. It is a slip that saints in all ages have made; they repented of it, saw its folly, and left that point alone for the future; and then the promise was fulfilled in its own due time. Let them, in such circumstances, go and do likewise, leaving the time entirely to the Lord.

3. An entire resignation as to the way and manner of bringing it about. As to the way of fulfilling the promise, we are ready to do just as we do with its time: to set a particular way for the Lord’s working it. And if that way is not kept, the proud heart takes offense: “But Naaman went away angry, saying, ‘I thought that he would surely come out, stand and call on the name of the Lord his God, and wave his hand over the spot’” (2 Kgs 5:11). But the Lord will have his people broken off from that too, so that they prescribe no way to him, but leave that to him entirely, as in that same case, verse 14: “So Naaman went down and dipped himself in the Jordan seven times, according to the word of the man of God … and he was clean.” The compass of our knowledge of ways and means is very narrow, so that if one way is blocked, we often cannot see another. But our God knows many ways of relief where we know only one, or none at all. And it is very usual for the Lord to bring the lifting up to his people in a way they had no view of, after repeated disappointments from those quarters from which they had great expectations.

4. Resignation as to the degree of the lifting up, yes, and as to its very taking place in time. The Lord will have his people so weaned that, however hasty they have sometimes been, insisting they must be lifted up soon and could bear it no longer, they will at length be brought to set no time at all. They will submit to go to the grave under their weight, if it seems good in the Lord’s eyes; and in that case they will be brought to be content with any measure of it in time, without prescribing how much: “If I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, He will bring me back … But if He should say, ‘I do not delight in you,’ then here I am; let Him do to me whatever seems good to Him” (2 Sam 15:25–26).

5. Continuing to pray and wait on the Lord in the case: “Pray in the Spirit at all times, with every kind of prayer and petition. To this end, stay alert with all perseverance” (Eph 6:18). It is pride of heart and an unsubdued spirit that make people give up praying and waiting because their humbling circumstances are drawn out time after time (2 Kgs 6:33). But due humility, going before the lifting up, brings men into the temper to pray, wait and hang on resolutely, setting no time for giving it up, till the lifting up comes, whether in time or in eternity (Lam 3:49–50).

Lastly, Mourning over mismanagements in the trial: “Surely I spoke of things I did not understand, things too wonderful for me to know” (Job 42:3). The proud heart dwells and enlarges on the man’s sufferings in the trial, spreads out all the folds of the trial on that side, and views them again and again. But when the Spirit of God comes duly to humble, in order to lifting up, he will make the man pass over, in a way, the suffering side of the trial, and turn his eyes on his own conduct in it. He will make him search it through, judge himself impartially and condemn himself, so that his mouth will be stopped.

This is the humility that goes before the lifting up in time, in the way of the promise.

II. We go on to consider the lifting up as brought about at the end of time, in the other world. And:

First, A word as to the nature of this lifting up. Concerning it we will say these five things.

1. This lifting up is certain in all cases of those humbled under humbling circumstances. Though one cannot, in every case, make them sure of a lifting up in time, yet they may be assured, whatever the case, that they will, beyond all doubt, get a lifting up on the other side: “Now we know that if the earthly tent we live in is dismantled, we have a building from God, an eternal house in heaven, not built by human hands” (2 Cor 5:1). Though God’s humbled children may both breakfast and dine on the bread of adversity and the water of affliction, they will be sure to sup sweetly and plentifully. And the believing expectation of the latter might serve to temper the former, and make them easy under it.

2. It will be a perfect lifting up (Heb 12:23). They will be perfectly delivered out of their particular trials and special furnace, whatever it was, that gave them many a weary day. Lazarus was then delivered from his poverty and sores, and from lying at the rich man’s gate (Luke 16:22), and fully delivered. Yes, they will then get a lifting up from all their humbling circumstances together. All the imperfections will then be at an end: inferiority in relationships, contradictions, afflictions, uncertainty and sin. If it was long in coming, there will be a blessed moment when they will get it all together.

3. They will not only be raised out of their low condition, but set up on high, as Joseph was not only brought out of prison, but made ruler over the land of Egypt. And they will be lifted up:

(1.) Into a high place: “The beggar died and was carried by the angels to Abraham’s side” (Luke 16:22). Now they are at best in a low place, only on this earth; there they will be seated in the highest heavens (Phil 1:23 with Eph 4:10). Often in their humbling circumstances they are now forced to embrace dunghills; then they will be set with Christ on his throne: “To the one who overcomes, I will grant the right to sit with Me on My throne” (Rev 3:21). Though their bellies now cling to the earth, and men say, “Bow down, so that we may walk over you,” they will then be settled in the heavenly mansions, above sun, moon and stars.

(2.) Into a high state and condition, a state of perfection. Out of all their troubles and uneasiness they will be brought into a state of rest. From their lowly and inglorious condition they will be advanced into a state of glory. Their burdened and sorrowful life will be followed by a fullness of joy. And instead of their humbling circumstances, they will be clothed with eternal glory and honor.

4. It will be a final lifting up, after which there will be no more casting down forever (Rev 7:16). When we get a lifting up in time, we are apt to imagine foolishly that we are at the end of our trials. But we soon find we were too hasty in our conclusions, and the cloud returns: “In prosperity I said, ‘I will never be shaken.’ … When You hid Your face, I was dismayed” (Ps 30:6–7). But then the trial will indeed be quite over, and the fight at an end; and then is the time of the reward and the triumph.

Lastly, Not the least uneasiness from the humbling circumstances will remain; on the contrary, they will have a glorious and desirable effect. I make no question that the saints will remember the humbling circumstances they were under here below. Did the rich man in hell remember that he had five brothers on the earth, how sumptuously he had fared, and how Lazarus sat at his gate? And can we doubt that the saints will remember their heavy trials perfectly (Rev 6:10)? But then they will remember them as waters that have dried up, as the man recovered to health remembers his tossings on the sickbed; and that way of remembering sweetens the present state of health beyond what it would otherwise be. Certainly the shore of the Red Sea was of all places the fittest to help the Israelites to sing in the highest key (Rev 15:3). And the humbling circumstances of saints on earth will be of the same use to them in heaven.

Secondly, A word on the due time of this lifting up. There is a particular, definite time for it in every saint’s case, which is the due time, but it is hidden from us. We can only say in general:

1. The due time for it is when the work we have to do in this world is over. God has appointed everyone their task, fight, trial and work, and until that is done, we are in a sense immortal (John 9:4; 11:9). That work is:

(1.) Doing work: work set for us by the great Master, to be done for the honor of God and the good of our fellow creatures (Eccl 9:10). We must be content to keep on doing, even in our humbling circumstances, until that is done to the end. It is not the due time for that lifting up until we are at the end of that work, and so have served our generation.

(2.) Suffering work. There is a certain portion of suffering allotted to the mystical body, and the head has divided its proportions among the several members. And it is not the due time for that lifting up until we have exhausted the share of it allotted to us. Paul looked on his life as a going on in that (Col 1:24).

2. When that lifting up comes, we will see that it has come exactly in the due time, and that it was well it came neither sooner nor later. For though heaven is always better than earth, and it would be better for us, absolutely speaking, to be in heaven than on earth, yet certainly there is a time in which it is better for the honor of God and his service that we be on the earth than in heaven: “But it is more necessary for you+ that I remain in the body” (Phil 1:24). And it will be no grief of heart to them, when they are there, that they were so long in their humbling circumstances and were not brought there sooner.

USE 1. Let not the humble, then, throw away their confidence, whatever their humbling circumstances may be. Let them assure themselves that a lifting up will come to them at length; if not here, then to be sure hereafter. Let them keep this in view and comfort themselves with it, for God has said it: “The needy will not always be forgotten” (Ps 9:18). Though the night were ever so long, the morning will come at length.

2. Let patience have its perfect work. The farmer waits for the return of his seed, the sea merchant for the return of his ships, the sheep farmer for what he calls year-time, when he draws in the produce of his flocks. All these have long patience; and why should not the Christian too have patience, and patiently wait for the time appointed for his lifting up?

You+ have heard much of the crook in the lot, and of the excellence of humbleness of spirit in a low lot over pride of spirit, even when joined with a high one. You+ have been called to humble yourselves+ in your+ humbling circumstances, and have been assured in that case of a lifting up. To conclude, we may assure ourselves that God will at length break the proud in pieces, however high they are; and he will triumphantly lift up the humble, however low they are.
